articles.author: Nshua Cali-Dibang
articles.title: Big Tech, AI, and the quiet expansion of digital surveillance in Nigeria
articles.excerpt: How much control do people retain over their personal information in a world increasingly shaped by AI?
articles.content:
This story by Nshua Cali-Dibang originally appeared on Global Voices. Text licensed under CC BY 3.0. Reformatted for reading; third-party media omitted.

How much control do people retain over their personal information in a world increasingly shaped by AI?

This post is part of Global Voices’ October 2026 Spotlight series, “Big Tech and Authoritarianism.” In this Spotlight, we explore how Big Tech facilitates and hinders authoritarian governments and practices, and how these choices influence the Global South. You can support this coverage by donating here.

Every search, social media interaction, and conversation with an artificial intelligence (AI) tool can leave behind information about its user. Individually, these digital traces may appear insignificant. Collectively, however, they can reveal interests, habits, preferences and patterns of behavior that have considerable commercial and political value.

As AI becomes increasingly embedded in everyday life, technology companies are finding new ways to use data to develop their products, personalize services and generate revenue. While these developments offer considerable benefits, they also raise a difficult question: How much control do people retain over their personal information in a world increasingly shaped by AI?

The issue extends beyond privacy policies and user agreements. It concerns the growing power of technology companies to collect information, draw conclusions about individuals, and influence the digital environments in which people communicate, work, and access information.

The business of knowing more about us

In September 2024, the United States Federal Trade Commission (FTC) published findings from an investigation into nine major social media and video-streaming companies, including Meta, YouTube, TikTok, and Amazon-owned Twitch.

The FTC reported that these companies collected extensive information about users and, in some cases, non-users. The information included personal details, interests, online activities, and data obtained from other sources. The investigation also raised concerns about lengthy data retention, inadequate privacy protections, and the use of personal information in automated systems, including AI.

The report highlighted a fundamental imbalance: Companies can accumulate substantial information about individuals, while those individuals may have limited understanding of how their data is used or how to prevent certain uses.

AI adds another dimension to this problem. Data can help train models, improve recommendations, and power automated decisions. However, the greater the volume and variety of information companies can access, the more important it becomes to establish clear limits on its collection and use.

The concern is not that every company collecting data is necessarily acting maliciously. Rather, it is that systems designed to maximize commercial value from information can create incentives to collect more data than people reasonably expect or understand.

Inclusion at what cost?

For millions of people, AI offers opportunities that were previously difficult to access. Students can use AI tools to support learning, small businesses can improve their operations, and journalists can explore new approaches to research and production.

In countries such as Nigeria, where access to resources and professional services can be uneven, these tools could help narrow certain gaps. AI systems that support local languages and reflect diverse cultural experiences could also make digital services more accessible.

Yet inclusion should mean more than allowing people to use a technology. It should also mean ensuring that they understand the conditions under which they use it and retain meaningful rights over their information.

Many digital services are governed by lengthy terms and privacy policies that users may accept without fully understanding the implications. Some AI products also raise questions about whether information submitted through prompts, uploaded documents, or other interactions may be retained or used to improve models.

The precise practices differ between companies and products. Nevertheless, users need clear explanations of what information is collected, why it is needed, how long it is retained, and whether it may be used for purposes beyond the immediate service.

Without these safeguards, the benefits of AI inclusion risk coming with an invisible cost: reduced control over personal information.

When corporate power begins to resemble surveillance

The connection between big tech and authoritarianism requires careful examination. Authoritarianism is not simply the collection of data by private companies. It involves the concentration and exercise of power in ways that undermine accountability, rights, and freedoms.

However, extensive corporate data collection can create conditions that make surveillance easier. Detailed personal information can support profiling, targeted persuasion and the prediction of individual behavior. Depending on the circumstances, businesses, governments, or other actors may exploit these capabilities.

The risks become particularly serious when personal data can be accessed or shared without adequate safeguards, when automated systems make consequential decisions without meaningful oversight, or when people have little opportunity to challenge how their information is used.

Concentrated corporate power adds another concern. When a small number of companies control widely used digital platforms, AI services, and large pools of information, individuals may have few practical alternatives. Leaving a platform may mean losing access to professional networks, customers, communities, or essential services.

This does not mean that every AI system is a surveillance tool or that every technology company intends to restrict freedom. It means that the infrastructure of digital life deserves scrutiny because its capabilities can be used in ways that extend beyond their original commercial purpose.

Nigeria’s data protection challenge

Nigeria has a legal framework intended to protect individuals against the misuse of their personal information. The Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 established the Nigeria Data Protection Commission and provides a framework for the lawful, fair and accountable processing of personal data.

Legislation is an important step, but effective protection also depends on implementation, public awareness, and regulators’ ability to hold organizations accountable.

As Nigerians increasingly adopt AI-powered services, questions about data governance become more pressing. Users need to understand their rights, while organizations must take responsibility for explaining their practices and protecting the information they collect.

There is also a wider question of representation. If AI systems are developed using data that inadequately reflects Nigerian languages, cultures, and social realities, their benefits may be distributed unevenly. Responsible AI governance must therefore address both the protection of personal information and the inclusion of communities whose experiences are often underrepresented.

UNESCO’s Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence emphasizes privacy, data protection, transparency, accountability, and fairness throughout the AI lifecycle. These principles provide a useful foundation for ensuring that technological progress respects human rights.

Innovation must not come at the expense of control

The challenge is not to reject AI or prevent companies from using data to develop useful technologies. It is to establish boundaries that allow innovation without making personal privacy an acceptable casualty.

Technology companies should minimize unnecessary data collection, communicate their policies clearly, provide meaningful choices, and strengthen protections against unauthorized access. Regulators must ensure that existing laws remain effective as AI capabilities evolve, while users need accessible information about the rights available to them.

Ultimately, digital inclusion cannot be measured solely by the number of people using AI. It must also consider whether those people can participate safely, understand the systems they rely on, and exercise meaningful control over their information.

As AI becomes more powerful, the question is no longer simply what technology can do with our data. It is who decides what can be done, who benefits from those decisions, and who has the power to challenge them.

The future of AI should not be defined only by what machines learn about us, but also by how much control we retain over ourselves.

Written by Nshua Cali-Dibang

articles.author: Rory Mir
articles.title: Google Forcing AI on Students Is BS
articles.excerpt: Google is rightfully facing blowback for forcing K-12 schools to enable AI if they wanted to keep using Google search. The company quickly backtracked and decoupled and turned off the services by default, but made it clear search will continue to be just another AI chatbot. This mandate forces an ultimatum on educators: accept generative AI or de-google your school.
articles.content:
Rory Mir · Electronic Frontier Foundation · CC BY 4.0

Google is rightfully facing blowback for forcing K-12 schools to enable AI if they wanted to keep using Google search. The company quickly backtracked and decoupled and turned off the services by default, but made it clear search will continue to be just another AI chatbot. This mandate forces an ultimatum on educators: accept generative AI or de-google your school.

Students, teachers, and parents across the U.S. are now years into an argument about how schools should respond to the growth of AI-enabled tools. Google decided to skip this debate and take this choice from schools. In August it activated AI chatbot Gemini for 150 million K-12 students on Google Classroom, leaving educators scrambling to respond. A few months later, Google introduced a new way to turn it off — but now administrators would also be turning off Google search.

Google walked this back somewhat, clarifying that Gemini, Gemini notebook, and Search will have their own controls and will be off by default. But because of Google’s broader approach to force AI on all search users, this change is still an example of a tech monopolist pushing unwanted changes into the classroom.

Tying AI to Search

It’s no secret that the biggest companies in AI  are operating at a huge loss, in the hope they can follow Uber’s enshittification playbook. Offer a cheap convenience at a major loss until old systems atrophy, then flip the script to reduce wages and raise consumer costs—whether that’s paying with cash or with data. 

This puts Google in the odd position of an incumbent, with around 90% of search traffic. It needs to not only make good on its own AI investment, but protect its dominance from new AI tools. It’s not just enough to offer its own AI mode, it needs to turn search into AI mode, while engaging in clumsy self-preferencing that is eating its own ad revenue.

The problem with this approach is the public is split on AI, to put it mildly. Some users will welcome these changes, but the rest are stuck in an all-or-nothing bargain. Anyone concerned  about the accuracy of AI overviews or their impact on click-through rates for online communities and small publishers can just deal with it. The bet is any inconvenience in switching to an alternative is enough to keep you trapped.

Google can and should offer a way to disable AI overviews. Smaller services like DuckDuckGo* and Brave search have simple and persisting AI settings which don’t require login. These services also don't mince words and make a distinction between generated AI summaries, suspected AI results, and the backend use of AI to curate links. 

It’s not enough to point to opaque workarounds, either. Adding “-ai” to your Google search will usually remove AI Overview, but so will “-unicorn”. This trick isn’t meant to be an AI off-switch, it’s a quirk of how AI Overview was implemented and can change at any time. These tricks also don’t generalize well to settings for system administrators. Hacks might work for now, but everyone—including administrators—deserve clear set-and-forget controls for the tools they rely on.

Pushing AI on Schools

De-googling your life isn’t easy, and for schools it can be even more difficult. For decades Google has gone after schools to foster life-long Google users—resulting in many institutions being deeply entrenched in its ecosystem despite data privacy concerns. That’s because schools face major switching costs when moving to a competitor. It takes more than flipping a setting—it means a lengthy contract process, staff retraining, and a cumbersome migration of past work. 

The difficulty of switching makes granular controls even more essential, particularly for a hot-button issue like generative AI. Few parents would send their kids to AI-driven schools, but they may want their kids to learn tools like search as they exist outside of the classroom. However, many parents and teachers concerned with AI disrupting learning are pushing major school districts to implement temporary AI moratoriums for young students. These pauses are meant to make sure any introduction of AI fits the needs of students and is done in a way that actually makes sure educators are prepared. 

But in either camp, this is a choice that must be made by schools, not Google. Teachers know more about what their students need than a trillion-dollar tech company, and this expertise should be respected in their own classrooms. 

Google’s self-preferencing and desperate attempt to eventually recoup on an AI money pit must be tempered with more fine-tune controls over generative AI. It’s in Google’s own interest to stop abusing its dominance to piss off users, advertisers, and school communities. It’s also Google’s responsibility as an adjudicated monopolist.

*DuckDuckGo is an EFF donor. EFF donors do not influence our agenda or our positions.

articles.author: David L. Chandler | Department of Chemical Engineering
articles.title: How to predict the behavior of molecules from scant data
articles.excerpt: A machine-learning approach called CheMeleon provides a practical way to develop new drugs or other molecules with much less detailed, expensive experimentation.
articles.content:
David L. Chandler | Department of Chemical Engineering · MIT News · MIT News republication policy

A machine-learning approach called CheMeleon provides a practical way to develop new drugs or other molecules with much less detailed, expensive experimentation.

Discovering new molecules for specific uses is a major driver of progress in a wide variety of industries, whether it’s pharmaceutical companies looking for new drugs, or electronics or energy companies seeking new materials with particular properties. But it’s also largely a trial-and-error process, because there is not yet any way to perfectly predict how a given chemical compound will behave in terms of the myriad different properties and responses materials can exhibit.

Recent progress has been made on using artificial intelligence and machine learning to supplement or speed up laborious calculations based on physical principles that can at least provide some initial guidance on which compounds might be worth synthesizing and testing. Now, a new method developed at MIT shows that when there are few data on some technologically relevant property, such as ligand affinities for a recently discovered cellular target for a potential drug, this approach can outperform other existing methods for winnowing down the field of possible molecules that might be worth looking at.

The findings were reported in the Sept. 14 issue of the Journal of Chemical Information and Modeling, in a paper by MIT graduate student Akshat Shirish Zalte and recent graduate Jackson Burns PhD ’26, Research Scientist Charlles Abreu, Professor William Green, and three researchers from the chemical company BASF. 

An earlier version of the paper has been online since last year, and the open-source model the team developed, called CheMeleon, has already found regular use by several pharmaceutical companies. CheMeleon was built using ChemProp, an open-source machine-learning package also developed and maintained by the Green group at MIT, and anyone can download CheMeleon through ChemProp and fine-tune it for their own purposes.

Earlier this year, there was a contest organized by OpenADMET for trying to predict the properties of a variety of new molecules that had not previously been synthesized, says Green, who is the Hoyt Hottel Professor of Chemical Engineering. “It was a big contest, a lot of people participated,” he says. When the winners were announced, it turned out that nine of the top 20 entries had used CheMeleon in their process. “So then we started getting all kinds of inquiries from the pharma companies about this, but our paper had just been submitted; it wasn’t even peer-reviewed or anything yet.”

While the paper went through that review process, its influence was already spreading. At least one pharma company, Green says, “sent a message to all their people, and said ‘Anytime you’re modeling a property, start with CheMeleon, that’s our new company policy’” when making initial decisions about which molecules to pursue.

The key to CheMeleon was pre-training a machine-learning model with detailed data about a million different molecules, so that it gets to learn correlations between the structure of a given molecule and how it behaves with respect to a catalog of about 1,600 descriptors that have been developed by chemists over decades. CheMeleon can then be fine-tuned to predict well-known properties like solubility and viscosity, to more esoteric properties such as bioactivity or reactivity, with a certain protein or enzyme.

Those million molecules are a minuscule fraction of the innumerable ways that atoms can bond together, but they provide enough examples so that once the AI system has been trained on them, it can work out on its own many underlying patterns and relationships, and then apply those to a new, unknown molecule that’s presented to it.

“Most of today’s deep-learning models require more data than traditional methods,” says Zalte. Some successful models use extensive data from the published literature in chemical journals, he says. “We don’t look at the literature at all. We just calculate a bunch of molecular descriptors like molecular weight or number of oxygens, among others.” Then predicting those descriptors forms the basis for their pre-training task.

CheMeleon is a pre-trained foundation model. Inspired by the well-known foundation models in language such as ChatGPT and Claide, which essentially are developed by feeding them massive amounts of information from the internet, CheMeleon uses molecular descriptors of a million molecules from PubChem, a large, freely available database of chemical information maintained by the U.S. National Institutes of Health. 

With classical expert-driven models, on the other hand, specialists in a field manually input detailed knowledge about their subject. In developing these classical models, he says, for example, people know from experiments that a certain property of interest, say solubility, may relate to particular descriptors of the same molecules, “like molecular weight, or the number of oxygens that are present, or how branchy or bulky the molecule is.” 

With this team’s approach, they can start with an existing neural network architecture and train it to learn underlying principles. “We’re not training it for a specific property, but as a general model that understands some level of chemistry, so that even if you fine-tune it with just a few data points for the task you care about, you can still get some good performance,” he says. That’s thanks to the fact that the model is “not having to learn everything from scratch.”

To verify its usefulness, “We compared our model not only against other foundation models that are out there, but also with classical models leveraging expert-designed principles,” Zalte says. Comparing its performance across 58 test cases, “we see that our model comes out on top.”

Green adds, “The CheMeleon foundation model drastically reduces the number of molecules that need to be tested experimentally to accurately predict the properties of new molecules. This is a huge advantage, since synthesizing and testing a large number of molecules is slow and expensive."

Besides the MIT members, the team also included Jochen Sieg, Christian Feldmann, and Miriam Mathea, researchers at BASF SE in Germany. The work was supported by the Machine Learning for Pharmaceutical Discovery and Synthesis consortium, along with fellowship support from U.S. Department of Energy and MathWorks.

articles.author: Paige Collings
articles.title: Presenting 'Desire Lines: Encoding Queer Digital Futures'
articles.excerpt: What does the digital future look like? Who gets to imagine it, shape it, and make it real?
articles.content:
Paige Collings · Electronic Frontier Foundation · CC BY 4.0

What does the digital future look like? Who gets to imagine it, shape it, and make it real?

Building a freer, more inclusive digital age requires not only challenging systems of surveillance and control, but also making space for creativity, community, and radical imagination. 

That's why earlier this year with the queer arts collective, we put out a call for submissions inviting people to explore the intersections of technology, identity, and digital liberation—whether that involved pointing the lens towards an underrepresented issue in digital justice efforts; sharing personal accounts of joy, pleasure, or sorrow under surveillance; or painting wide imaginations for our communities using technology for good instead of carcerality and doom.

And we’re excited to share that the project is now live! Desire Lines: Encoding Queer Digital Futures explores a digital world that dreams wilder and exists louder. Seven artists share their visions of digital liberation, spanning from early internet-coded yearning to escapist steamy chat rooms and seed-laced battle suits for revolution. 

These essays and stories remind us that digital rights aren't just about the existence of technology and its deployment as existing in a vacuum, but instead about how tech tools are a way for people to express themselves freely, find communities, explore identities, and build spaces to exist and seek joy without fear. Too often, conversations about technology focus on innovation, efficiency, and the next big thing while overlooking the people and communities most affected by the systems being built. This project was an effort to break containment and make space for something different: a chance to imagine digital futures rooted in queer creativity, resistance, and possibility.

Together with the queer arts collective, we were excited to launch the magazine and celebrate the artists and ideas that brought it to life through our session at Mozilla Festival last week, ‘Privacy x Queer Desire,’ where we started out by co-curating a community privacy plan grounded in digital fairness before launching the magazine. 

If the stories in Encoding Queer Digital Futures teach us one thing, it’s that we don't have to accept the digital future handed to us by oppressive governments and tech companies. We already have pre-Big Tech internet experiences encoded in our fondest memories that can inform our dreams for something better, and together we can build a new reality.

Read Desire Lines: Encoding Queer Digital Futures here.

articles.title: Spacewalk Cleanup, Biomedical Science, and Maintenance Wrap Up Week
articles.excerpt: The seven Expedition 75 crew members cleaned up after a spacewalk, conducted biomedical assessments, and maintained orbital systems to wrap up a busy week aboard the International Space Station.
articles.content:
The seven Expedition 75 crew members cleaned up after a spacewalk, conducted biomedical assessments, and maintained orbital systems to wrap up a busy week aboard the International Space Station.

Flight engineers Joshua Kutryk of CSA (Canadian Space Agency) and Anil Menon of NASA reconfigured spacesuits and stowed spacewalking tools inside the Quest airlock following Thursday’s six-hour and 59-minute spacewalk. Kutryk and Menon finalized a years-long effort to increase the orbital outpost’s power generation capacity from 160 kilowatts to 215 kilowatts, or about 30%, when they installed the eighth roll-out solar array on the space station’s truss structure.

On Friday, the pair refilled spacesuit water tanks, removed air bubbles from the tanks, then installed rechargeable batteries inside the suits to continue keeping astronauts safe and comfortable during future spacewalks. Kutryk and Menon also cleaned up the Quest airlock, inspected tools and spacesuits, stowed the gear inside protective covers, and ensured all spacewalk-supporting equipment was powered down.

The experienced spacewalkers also joined NASA flight engineers Jessica Watkins and Luke Delaney for a post-spacewalk conference with engineers on the ground. The quartet discussed their perspectives that will help prepare astronauts and mission controllers for future excursions outside the orbital outpost.

Watkins and Delaney assisted the spacewalkers in and out of their spacesuits, monitored their activities, and operated the Canadarm2 robotic arm on Thursday. The NASA duo also helped out with the spacewalk cleanup tasks on Friday. All four astronauts fit in a couple of hours each in their Friday schedule to relax following a week filled with science, maintenance, and spacewalking duties.

In the Roscosmos segment of the orbiting complex, flight engineer Sergey Teteryatnikov focused on biomedical research during his shift at the end of the week. Teteryatnikov first measured his blood pressure using arm, wrist, and finger cuffs. Next, he jogged on the Zvezda service module’s treadmill while attached to electrodes measuring his heart and breathing rate. The continuous health data helps researchers monitor and understand how microgravity affects a crew member’s cardiorespiratory system.

Flight engineer Anna Kikina worked throughout the day servicing Roscosmos ventilation systems and scientific payload hardware. Station commander Pyotr Dubrov completed an overnight carbon dioxide monitoring session, downloaded the data to mission controllers on Earth, then inspected the condition of modules and hatches.

Learn more about station activities by following the space station blog, @space_station on X, as well as the ISS Facebook and ISS Instagram accounts.

articles.title: The Gunslingers of White Sands
articles.excerpt: From Earth orbit to the Moon and Mars, explore the world of human spaceflight with NASA each week on the official podcast of the Johnson Space Center in Houston, Texas. Listen to in-depth conversations with the astronauts, scientists and engineers who make it possible.
articles.content:
From Earth orbit to the Moon and Mars, explore the world of human spaceflight with NASA each week on the official podcast of the Johnson Space Center in Houston, Texas. Listen to in-depth conversations with the astronauts, scientists and engineers who make it possible.

On episode 444, Houston We Have a Podcast kicks off a new series in collaboration with NASA’s White Sands Test Facility, introducing producer and host Kathryn Martinez and exploring the facility’s role in advancing human spaceflight. This episode was recorded on October 7, 2026.

Transcript

Gary Jordan

Houston We Have a Podcast. Welcome to the official podcast of the NASA Johnson Space Center, Episode 444: The Gunslingers of White Sands. I’m Gary Jordan, and I’ll be kicking off this episode today. On this podcast, we bring in the experts, scientists, engineers, and astronauts, all to let you know what’s going on in the world of human spaceflight and more.

This episode is a special one as it kicks off what will be a series hosted on Houston We Have a Podcast in collaboration with the agency’s White Sands Test Facility in Las Cruces, New Mexico. This is a little-known satellite site of NASA that has a big impact on advancing human spaceflight. Some would say a hypervelocity impact, and we’ll get into why that’s a great pun in a minute.

This series will be a bit of a departure from our traditional style, but we’re excited to try something new and explore the capabilities of this incredible facility. To help kick us off before we get into the heart of the episode, I’m pleased to welcome the producer and host of the White Sands series, Kathryn Martinez.

Kathryn, welcome to Houston We Have a Podcast!

Kathryn Martinez

Hi, Gary. Thanks so much for having me on the show today. All of us at White Sands are absolutely thrilled to be working with you all on this.

Gary Jordan 

We’re thrilled as well. We’re thrilled as well, and we’re introducing you. So, so Katheryn, if you don’t mind, tell us a little bit about yourself, your background, what you do at White Sands.

Kathryn Martinez

Sure. So, I’m a technical writer and editor at the White Sands Test Facility, but my background is really in storytelling. So I went to New Mexico State University here in Las Cruces, where I studied broadcasting. So radio was actually like one of my first exposures to storytelling. And then I ended up going to the University of Oregon for my master’s in journalism, and that’s when I kind of transitioned to, like gravitated more towards long form storytelling, specifically in print.

After that, I worked as a television news producer in Albuquerque, which it’s a pretty big market and a very different environment from cities like Las Cruces or Eugene, which are well small towns. And I was assigned the sort of classic rookie overnight shift producing for the morning show. So it’s very unglamorous, monitoring police scanners, watching for breaking news things, things things like that.

And about a year later, I went to the University of Leeds in England, where I studied creative writing. I was really drawn to literary fiction, world building, and not in like the fantasy sense of world building, but making a place feel real for a reader who’s never been somewhere. Because obviously, in fiction, that that place doesn’t exist. But making it feel alive and textured and curious, so that’s I sort of blended journalism with that you know creative fiction aspect of writing. And then I ended up at at NASA. It’s sort of a interesting but a serendipitous sort of long spiraling journey. But as you can see, I came to White Sands with no aerospace background whatsoever.

So my primary role is technical writing and editing, mostly test documents, job instructions. But then I started getting opportunities to tell stories about the mission and about people that started in contractor communications quarterly newsletter, and then eventually through articles with NASA.gov. And eventually that evolved into asking what those stories could be in in audio format. So my role has really expanded in the nearly three years that I’ve been here at White Sands.

Gary Jordan   

And it sounds like a lot of the things that you seem to be passionate about, right? You’re you’re exploring these fringe communities, exploring what’s what are the untold stories, right? It sounds like you’ve taken a creative spin on that with the creative writing experience that you have. This seems like, I mean I’m very excited because what you’re describing in terms of what your passionate about is what we’re about to explore. The technical writing, of course, is essential but, this is a time to shine in terms of creativity and it seems like that’s where a lot of your a lot of your passions ride, and you’re doing it in a lot of different ways. Catherine, we’ve been talking more than a year about podcasting. I know we’ve connected quite a bit ago to talk about exactly how to approach this. You say you came from you came from you know radio was one of those first passions, and so talk about the inspiration for for pursuing a podcast and audio storytelling as part of you know sharing the White Sands story.

Kathryn Martinez

Yeah, so the initial push toward a podcast, it really came from Anthony Quitario. He is a photographer here at White Sands, and he and I both had radio experience at New Mexico State University. Anthony was actually the station’s music director, and so we ended up all these years later working at at White Sands, and so he’s the one that really saw that opportunity that we should get on board with this, you know, multimedia and get ourselves out there in a way that just hadn’t been done before. And I had already been writing the articles, so I kind of started to sculpt what a podcast would look like from an editorial perspective. What it would sound like, how we could structure things, and and what my role in them would be.

You know, a lot of a lot of journalists say they go into the field because they want to give people a voice, but everyone already has a voice. So it’s it’s kind of just my job and my I guess philosophy is to go into this world, figure out what fascinates me about it, and hopefully that resonates with others, and we can actually bring listeners inside of this world. And yeah, so keeping that feeling of curiosity that lived in real world experience, we we want the audience to discover everything with us in real time. And we wanted the recording to actually reflect that, so we used like a combination of lapel mics and 360 ambient mics. So we’re trying to be flies on the wall, and just we spent a day in the hypervelocity test lab, and these are real tests that you’re going to hear them doing real conversations, unfiltered, the machinery, the buzz of the room, everything unfolding as it was. We didn’t, you know, sit down afterward and ask them to explain.

So, you know, we’re doing this also with a really small team. For this episode, it’s Fernando Morales, and he is our multimedia specialist. He actually has only been at White Sands for two months, three months, something like that? And so, when we recorded this story in September, he had only been here about a month and a half. So, I’m doing the reporting, hosting, writing, kind of shaping that framework, and then he’s really bringing the audio side of it to life.

And if we, you know, if we can get people interested in learning more about aerospace, learning more about hypervelocity, whatever topic it is we’re covering, you know, we’re not here to give a seminar or a lecture. We’re here to spark that curiosity. So that’s kind of our approach.

Gary Jordan

I am very excited because the approach is a little bit unique, and I do want to like position it for our listenership. You know, we’re having this conversation right now just to really couch it. But what we’re about to hear is is a very different style. This is the narrative approach. You’re going and you’re and you’re really telling that story. You are narrating it. You’re hearing the background noise. And it’s called The Gunslingers of White Sands because you’re going to hear what sound like gunshots because they’re really firing these projectiles to really understand how they interact with with certain materials and things. And of course, you could probably explain it a little bit better than me. But but it’s a it’s a unique style. You know you have experience of radio you know you and it’s and you said Fernando did as well and so between between you guys having that experience and thinking about well what’s our approach to audio storytelling going to be you know what were some of your inspirations for this particular style?

Kathryn Martinez 

Sure, so initially we had sort of done a pilot episode where we had a traditional sit-down podcast, and after further discussion, we felt that that just couldn’t was not the best way to introduce the world to White Sands, because, as you’ll hear, even in this episode, there are people. Most of the people who work here now, had never heard of this test site, had never heard of the facility until they actually started working there. So, having a sit-down conversation under, I guess, sort of like the premise that people understand, you know, for Houston We Have a Podcast people understand what Johnson Space Center is, but they don’t know they’ve never heard of White Sands Test Facility, right? So we needed to create a style where we could actually pull people into that world and walk them through with us from basically square one, knowing nothing.

So we were kind of inspired by you know shows like This American Life, that that very classic narrative storytelling approach where you know you do have a host kind of guiding you through. I personally was very inspired by like Louis Theroux taking these you know, kind of weird, wacky worlds and and making them accessible because ultimately accessibility is that’s really the name of the game for us. We want to make we want to bring people in. We want to not even bring people in. We want to take this world to people. We want to take this place that people can’t normally go, and we want to give them an all-access pass, an all-access look at this as much as we possibly can.

These test personnel don’t typically get the spotlight. They’re not used to being in the spotlight. They don’t particularly care. That’s not why they do it. They you know they want to do this for the they’re doing this for the greater good of humanity and for the mission, it’s always mission first, and so you know these are not people used to being in the public eye at all, and so that’s why taking this narrative broadcast approach was really important, so that we could give that authentic look rather than a sit down approach where people are maybe a little out of their natural environment and prefer to do the work, and they’re so passionate about the work they do that it’s very easy to get them to tell us about what they’re doing and share that world with us as they’re actually in it and living it.

Gary Jordan

I love it. Part of it is, and you recognize, right? This is this is not a this is not a widely known site. So you’re taking the approach, thinking, well, let’s introduce the listenership to White Sands. Let’s give that overall aspect of what it is.

This specific episode looks at hypervelocity impacts, and like we said, this is series, so we’re going to continue to work with you and explore different aspects of the facility. But but this is the introductory episode, and so with that, Kathryn, if you don’t mind giving us just a high level of, we’re about to explore White Sands. How would you how would you describe it to someone who doesn’t really know what this facility is? Where is it? What does it look like? What happens there? Right? What’s the introduction to White Sands?

Kathryn Martinez

Sure, so, White Sands fundamentally, it’s a hazardous test facility, primarily supporting human spaceflight, and there’s just in. Incredible range of expertise out here. Our core capabilities are rocket propulsion, oxygen systems, hypervelocity impact testing, propellants and aerospace fluids, COPVs Composite Overwrapped Pressure Vessels, flight acceptance testing, spaceflight component services, and then we also have tons of supporting capabilities here. WSTF is really its own little ecosystem. We have our own fire department. We have our own environmental department.

We are we’re here in the middle of the desert, so even wildlife safety is deeply ingrained and incorporated into our training out here because we’re sharing this space with coyotes, rattlesnakes, road runners- you know, all the critters that we have to coexist with. So it’s not the typical NASA that I think a lot of people have in their minds. It’s not the crisp suit, skinny tie, Apollo era. There’s you know cowboy boots worn in jeans. You know people are people are here operating in in a in a hazardous environment.

And this the spirit of White Sands is- it’s almost like this. There’s almost an outlaw spirit. You know, we talk about the the name of the episode, The Gunslingers of White Sands, and that was really drawn from the feeling you get when you arrive here. It’s almost this frontier outpost. It’s this very strange mixture, like simultaneously sci-fi futurism and 1960s minimalism, so it’s it’s almost uncanny. You’re you’re out in the middle of nowhere, and in this episode, you’ll hear I will take you driving in to the facility with me down the long long access road until you get to the security gate, and even when you get past that, you keep going for several miles. And depending on where you need to go, you may need to access back roads, or I mean, there’s it’s easy to get lost out here, and you you really are in the middle of nowhere. And I guess the simplest way I could describe it is a very spread out neighborhood with white buildings, and aesthetically the site just hasn’t changed much since it opened. But of course, inside these unassuming buildings, this phenomenal advancements in aerospace is taking place.

Gary Jordan

That’s fantastic, and I need to go out there myself. The way you’re describing it, it sounds fantastic. It reminds me a little bit of when I visit the Kennedy Space Center. It has that sort of same vibe, where it’s these long stretches of road, and you need to go to a building, and you’re driving for miles and miles. You’re like, man, this thing is huge. Definitely something that I think is is worth exploring. And like you said, we’re gonna all these different aspects of White Sands. We’re going to explore as part of this series. Very very excited.

Today, like you said, you talked about the gunslingers, which is a nod to a little bit of the culture, a little bit of the vibe that’s there, but then also the testing itself. And the first test we’re going to explore is hyper velocity impact. We’re going to get right into it as part of this episode, but give us a little preview of of hypervelocity impact, what it is, why it’s important to lead us into this this narrative storytelling that we’re just about to hear.

Kathryn Martinez

Sure. So as I mentioned, hypervelocity is one of White Sands’, and actually, really, the people here you’ll hear them call it WSTF. WSTF: White Sands Test Facility, because of course we love to speak in acronyms. So hypervelocity is one of WSTF’s core capabilities, and so the basic problem is you know spacecraft can encounter micrometeoroids and orbital debris. They’re moving at these extraordinary velocities, and our team here uses specialized guns called two stage light gas guns to recreate those impacts here on Earth, so that we can understand what happens to spacecraft materials and hardware in those harsh conditions.

Yeah, and so a little bit more too on the the gunslinger thing, in the lab there there are three guns. There’s the one inch, the 17 cal, and then the 50 cal, and those are all dependent on the size of of projectiles that are being fired, as you’ll hear in the episode. But beneath the 17 caliber trigger, there’s actually a sticker of Doc Holliday, you know, Young Guns under underneath the trigger, it’s a very yeah on the nose nod to sort of the Wild West culture. It feels like you’re in this sort of outlaw environment. I mean, in a metaphorical sense, of course, with just guns and bunkers, and you know the hypervelocity lab. Even comparatively, even though everything else is is so remote. It’s the remote hyper velocity test lab, and it is even you know more distant from other buildings here, and even that is its own ecosystem in itself, because it is one of our core capabilities.

So there’s a rather large team of engineers, of techs, there are our photographers out there as well.

And so it’s a yeah, it’s a very it’s a it’s a warehouse in the middle of the desert. There’s really no no fancier way to describe it than that. But you know what happens inside is it’s it’s mind blowing, honestly. And the speeds, you know, seven kilometers a second, and and that doesn’t even reach the Orbital velocities outside of like that’s low Earth orbit velocity, so things can be moving even faster than that. And so you’ll hear the experts talk about all the all the ins and outs of of those details. But it’s it’s really phenomenal stuff.

And another interesting thing too about White Sands and just Las Cruces in general is it’s that you know we’re here in the borderland, so we have a very a very you know big international community. So you’ll you’ll hear that too. You know several of the engineers in this episode- bilingual, and you’ll you’ll get to hear from them. And that’s a really wonderful like cultural melding that we have here. That’s really unique to not just the city of Las Cruces, but our particular NASA site.

Gary Jordan

Fantastic, and I think this is this is fantastic because even as you mentioned the the Hypervelocity Lab, you know we’re talking about White Sands, but you say it’s it’s a building off to the side. So really, we’re exploring White Sands, and we’re be and we’re beginning in this very interesting place. And there’s a lot more to explore. Kathryn, I love your style. I’m very happy to work together on this and introduce the site to our audience. This is the first episode in our White Sands series: The Gunslingers of White Sands.

Let’s get right into it. Enjoy.

Kathryn Martinez  

I’m in a bunker beneath the White Sands Test Facility’s remote hypervelocity test lab, asking myself the same question engineer Paula Rodriguez asked when she started two years ago.

Paola Rodriguez

But having a bunker is- it could be like, wow, what is this? Am I gonna die, or you know?

Kathryn Martinez

A valid concern. I wouldn’t be the first thing to die in here, but I take my chances and find a seat in the corner beside a small graveyard of beetle shell and lizard skin.

Cozy.

You’d think it was the end of the world. Bare concrete, flickering fluorescent lights, gas masks slung over office chair armrests. If not for the monitors, the closest thing we have to windows, showing a perfectly blue New Mexico sky.

Announcer

Attention, all personnel in the 272 area. The 272 area. is now in red status.

Kathryn Martinez 

And then there’s that.

Paola Rodriguez

Okay, red status. We use it here in Hyper to notify people that we’re doing testing. Pretty much, what it means is that no one can enter, no one can leave.

Kathryn Martinez 

Looks like I’m not going anywhere. And Paula assures me there’s nowhere else I’d rather be.

Paola Rodriguez 

The bunker allows allow us to make this hazardous testing and make us feel secure. Overwhelmed, but secure. You know because it’s like, oh, what? What is this? This is just in the movies. So it’s fun.

Kathryn Martinez

Quite the turnaround from. “Am I gonna die?”

Secure is exactly what we need. In a few seconds, a giant chemical gun is going to fire-a fact nobody seems particularly nervous about. Because for the team at White Sands, it’s not the end of the world. Just another day at the office.

Say hello to Alan Davis.

Alan Davis 

Hellooo.

Kathryn Martinez

He’s a leading expert on hypervelocity, visiting from Johnson Space Center.

Alan Davis 

You need a taco. By the way, it’s $1.29 now. It’s no longer 99 cents. Don’t know how I know that.

Kathryn Martinez

And while Alan may not be able to explain his knowledge of fast food taco inflation, he can tell you a thing or two about:

Alan Davis 

Rocket sciences, man! You know, meteoroid material has a, you know, like high and low densities ratio. Meteoroid material can be a bit rocky.

Kathryn Martinez 

But if you’re like the rest of us, like me, none of this probably makes much sense yet.

Chances are you’ve never even heard of the White Sands test facility, which is fine. Neither had most of the people who work here.

Probably helps to know where here is. Head eastbound down U.S. Route 70, leaving behind Las Cruces, a dusty college town and retirement community in southern New Mexico, with little to suggest what’s tucked away in the desert beyond. On the outskirts, the jagged Organ Mountains frame a smattering of roadside outposts. Keep driving past the odd auto shop or cafe. Hard to tell if any of them are actually still in business until even those disappear. Exit at NASA Road, a long stretch of asphalt with the 360 view of absolutely nothing. A few miles of highway hypnosis later, it’s time to badge in at the security gate. Without the proper credentials, this is where the drive ends.

Security Guard 

Good morning.

Kathryn Martinez

Fortunately, mine check out, and I’m waved through, moving off the main drag and onto a network of winding gravel back roads. And that’s when I see it-a plain building against the hills. On the roof, a lone orange windsock flutters in the afternoon breeze, like a sandcastle someone stuck a flag in. This somehow is the remote hypervelocity test lab. They aren’t kidding about the remote part. From the outside, it doesn’t look like much. Inside-

Paola Rodriguez

Pretty unique. I mean, even though the lab is like a big warehouse, you can say that.

Kathryn Martinez

Okay, so the inside isn’t much to look at either. It’s a warehouse with giant metal tubes. But those tubes-they’re two-stage light gas guns, devices used to simulate the impact of micrometeoroids and orbital debris.

Paola Rodriguez 

We have three here in our lab:

Kathryn Martinez 

The .17 caliber, the .50 caliber, and the one inch, whose range extends beyond the building. But that’s not on today’s agenda.

Paola Rodriguez

I mean, probably people are familiar with the regular guns, but when you talk about two-stage light gas guns, it’s like, what is that?

Kathryn Martinez

Yeah, what is that? Paola’s read my mind.

Paola Rodriguez

Pretty much a system that divides in two. Right?

Kathryn Martinez 

Sounds easy enough.

Daniel Rodriguez

The two-stage light gas gun principles introduce an intermediate high-pressure compression stage.

Kathryn Martinez 

Uh… Nevermind.

Daniel Rodriguez 

It uses a piston stage to compress a low molecular…

Kathryn Martinez

That’s Daniel Rodriguez. No relation to Paola, by the way. He’s a jack of all trades engineer.

Daniel Rodriguez 

Combusting thermite… underground coal gasification… decomposing ammonia brain to produce hydrogen.

Kathryn Martinez

With a resume that can make a sci-fi supervillain jealous.

Daniel Rodriguez 

Induction heaters… very high voltage stuff… designing magnetic fields… laser ignition systems…

Kathryn Martinez

Even with that toolkit, hypervelocity doesn’t just… come naturally.

Daniel Rodriguez 

Obviously, like hyper used my my my background, but at the same time, I had to learn a lot new stuff. You know, because hypervelocity is very specialized.

Kathryn Martinez 

Just how specialized?

Daniel Rodriguez 

I would say like 50 people, less than 100, to be honest. Obviously, there’s a lot of people working around it, but people who truly understand the technology at a high level, I think I think very few people in the world.

Kathryn Martinez 

Daniel is one of them.

Daniel Rodriguez 

Yeah. So basically, here we have two-stage gas guns. The idea, the concept of these guns is to first you want to remove the atmosphere. We have vacuum pumps that pull the air out, and then we fill the pump tube with hydrogen, which is the lightest gas available. The lighter the gas, the higher the speed of sound you can reach. So, two-stage gas guns tend to use either hydrogen or helium. However, in in our case, you want to go to hydrogen because you can even get higher velocities with hydrogen.

Kathryn Martinez

Those velocities typically land between six and eight kilometers a second, with the .50 cal clocking in at seven kilometers a second.

Daniel Rodriguez 

And you also install a burst disc that bursts at a specific static pressure, and that one is fully engineered based on the output velocity that you want to get. And then you compress the hydrogen to really high pressures, and then you will burst the pedal valve, and then that that the gas will decompress like a spring.

Kathryn Martinez

In his ten years at White Sands, Daniel’s research on light gas guns has taken him across the world, but around these parts, well, ten years is nothing.

Paola Rodriguez

One of the things that I was surprised-they have been working for a long, a lot of years here, twenty-five years, something like that.

Kathryn Martinez

That would be veteran gunner Dennis Garcia. I find Dennis at a microscope. Brushing something with a sort of tiny toothbrush tool.

Dennis Garcia 

Okay, right now I’m inspecting a sabot for the .50 cal gun range.

Kathryn Martinez 

A sabot, a secure carrier for the projectile.

Dennis Garcia 

I’m looking for cracks on the Lexan or pieces that don’t fit together right because we need them to separate correctly after we shoot them,

Kathryn Martinez

It’s delicate work. The projectile this sabot will carry is just 1.7 millimeters across, about the width of the tip of a ballpoint pen. Depending on what conditions they’re trying to simulate, the projectile can be made from different materials like aluminum alloys or glass. This is where size matters.

Dennis Garcia

If they want a big projectile shot, they go to the one inch, and if they want a medium-sized projectile shot, they do it on the .50 cal, and if they have a small projectile, they go ahead and do that on the .17 cal. So it all matters of the size of projectile that we’re requested to shoot.

Kathryn Martinez 

I think I’m starting to understand.

First:

Dennis Garcia 

It all starts out with a powder charge at the breech of a what’s called the pump tube, where hydrogen gas is held.

Kathryn Martinez 

And then:

Dennis Garcia

The projectile is released from that sudden pressure burst of pressure. So that’s the second stage of the gun.

I’ve always loved science, especially when I learned about the space shuttle. I would build models of the shuttle, never dreaming that I would actually be doing testing for the shuttle. It’s a it’s a dream come true.

Kathryn Martinez

All this time, Dennis hasn’t lost sight of that bigger picture.

Dennis Garcia

You can get into a mind frame where where you’re doing it, and then you’re not thinking of the end product of what you’re doing, meaning how important it is to do this testing.

Kathryn Martinez 

And the stakes are only getting higher.

Daniel Rodriguez 

Spacecraft they use maneuvers to try to avoid overall debris impact, but because overall debris keeps growing every year, it is predicted that at one point in time we’re gonna, they’re gonna run out of maneuvers, and the probability of spacecraft being impacted by orbital debris is gonna reach one hundred percent.

Kathryn Martinez 

In short:

Paola Rodriguez 

Biggest dumpster that we have here on Earth is space right now.

Kathryn Martinez

And in that floating junkyard full of the leftovers of human spaceflight, even a fleck of paint can rip through hardware.

Today’s testing will recreate what happens when orbital debris collides with a spacecraft. At seven kilometers a second, you could travel from Houston to Las Cruces in about three minutes.

Faster than a speeding bullet.

Daniel Rodriguez 

This projectiles will traveling like five times faster than a bullet.

Alan Davis 

The projectiles aren’t moving like a bullet. They’re moving so much faster. They’re almost I want to say plastic?

Kathryn Martinez 

A lot faster.

Alan Davis

Well, the impact, depending on what it’s impacting and what the impactor is, kind of speaks to how it shocks when it hits and the mechanics of, of what the shield can do.

Daniel Rodriguez 

And we’ve shot like bulletproof vests, and at seven kilometers per second, and they don’t even work.

Kathryn Martinez 

That’s the challenge: shielding missions from the unthinkable. So in the lab, how do you spot a threat moving that fast?

That’s Art Pardo’s job, the electronic specialist behind the lens of three ultra high-speed cameras.

Art Pardo 

So we have cameras that are able to record at 200 million frames a second. We have others that are 10 million frames a second, and we have others that are 1.3 million frames a second.

Kathryn Martinez 

They’re all trained on Old Blue, the 50 caliber, a massive blue cylinder with a submarine-looking hatch at one end. Art tells me some of its parts were repurposed. In a past life, Old Blue was dough-mixing equipment at a bakery factory.

As for Art, he’s managed to stay in one piece. He’s been here for 20 years.

Art Pardo 

Any any any any program that that that involves NASA, we had a hand in it. Of course, we do a lot of testing even before the mission is starts. So, like we’re working on future missions right now.

Kathryn Martinez 

Not as long as Dennis, but long enough to see a lot change.

Art Pardo

It changed from enormously. High speed, for instance, we started with regular IR film with a camera system called a coin camera, which is just basically a laser going through the tank, being the image being being put onto the film by a little beryllium mirror turner at 3,000 RPM. So, from regular, to to digital, to high speed, of course, high speed digital, and then. And then even ultra high speed digital.

Announcer 

Attention, all personnel in the 272 area.

Kathryn Martinez 

But that sound, the amber warning, has always meant one thing: get to the bunker.

Announcer 

The lab area are now in amber status.

Kathryn Martinez 

It’s a full house down here. The entire test crew, me, my audio guy Fernando, and Alan.

Alan Davis 

Hyper velocity. Do you…?

Kathryn Martinez

Who, while we’re on the subject of orbital debris, explains to me that hypervelocity isn’t hyper enough.

Alan Davis

You know, on orbit, 50 kilometers, 15 kilometers a second, 70 kilometers, depending on, you know, so we could never test as fast as it is on orbit.

Kathryn Martinez

Daniel’s working on fixing that.

Daniel Rodriguez

So right now, with the two-stage gas guns, we’re pretty much capped at eight kilometers per second. Like Alan was saying, there’s orbital debris that travels at higher velocities than that. The problem right now is that a lot of models extrapolate. In extrapolation, there’s a risk with extrapolation because you’re trying to model realms that haven’t been proven by with testing.

So the idea is to develop the technology, which right now we’re trying to push for a three-stage gas gun, which is a two-stage with an extra pump tube. So we’ll have two, two pump tubes and a barrel. So that’s the long-term goal. That’s what the aim is right now.

Kathryn Martinez 

For now, two stages will have to do.

Announcer 

The two seven two area is now in red status.

Dennis Garcia 

All right, hit of number 26205. Bit dV. Our target angle is 45 degrees. We’re shooting a stainless steel 1.7 millimeter.

Kathryn Martinez

I’m not entirely sure what to expect, so I braced myself.

Dennis Garcia

3… 2…

Kathryn Martinez

The results are nominal, exactly what they’re supposed to be. Which, after hours of setup, feels almost anticlimactic. But you see, you have to be very, very good for something so extreme to feel this boring,

Alan Davis

Our colleagues here at White Sands are probably the leading edge of that. They they have a very high success ratio, which we like, very repeatable, which helps with your equation development.

You know, I’ve I’ve seen other facilities. I wouldn’t say in in a good way. I’d say struggle trying to you know get things to work properly. Folks here have been doing this for 30 plus years now. Gone down and experienced a lot of the bumps in the road, and have you know crossed those bumps.

Kathryn Martinez

I’m amazed, and I’ll admit a little relieved, but we’re still stuck down here while the techs donning gas masks head upstairs to clear the carcinogenic aftermath of the shot.

Dennis Garcia 

You see us put these masks on. Hold your breath.

Kathryn Martinez 

We’re given the green light.

Announcer 

The gun lab and 272 area are now in green status.

Kathryn Martinez

Literally, I’ve made it out alive, which everyone here will tell you was always the plan. At the hypervelocity lab, safety comes before anything else.

Art Pardo 

Everything we we do is is in a safe manner. Our safety documents built into our procedures, so so we we’re able to maintain the same level of safety every time we do the shop. We we do we do it the same way.

Kathryn Martinez

It’s part of the reputation White Sands has been building since 1963, when the facility was established to support the Apollo program. 30 years later, in 1993, the Hypervelocity Test Lab was added to the site.

Dennis Garcia

Aerospace-it’s highly known because of the testing that we do here. We’re getting a lot of recognition.

Kathryn Martinez 

Among those taking notice? Some pretty high-profile names.

Jared Isaacman

Thank you very much for the question. This is this is a subject that I’m pretty passionate about…

Kathryn Martinez

That’s NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman speaking during his first confirmation hearing. In 2022 Isaacman came to this very lab where the team tested extravehicular suit materials for his Polaris Dawn spacewalk.

Jared Isaacman 

I had an opportunity to visit the the NASA facility and see what a one and two millimeter piece of aluminum does at near orbital velocities, and I can tell you what it penetrates through is pretty- It’s it’s it’s eye opening to say the least.

Kathryn Martinez

And then it hits me: this is real. There are people in space right now getting ready to go, whose lives depend in part on the work happening here, work being done by people whose names the world may never know, and that’s okay with them.

Daniel Rodriguez 

It’s work that we do and has value to humanity, and that’s that’s something that I feel really proud of, and I’m pretty sure all the people in here in this lab feels proud about that too.

Paola Rodriguez

Every job is important. And every job matters, but but here, like having a mission and want to help the future per se, it’s it’s really cool.

Kathryn Martinez 

Later that afternoon, we’re gearing up for a test on the fastest gun in the lab, .17 caliber. There’s no bunker, just a yellow box painted on the concrete marking the safe zone, and it’s not Dennis at the trigger this time.

Dennis Garcia

Try to pass that along as much as I can. the The knowledge of the years that I’ve been here, and to make things easier for the next generation of gunners that come along.

Kathryn Martinez 

It’s Shane, a young gunner who’d rather let the .17 cal do the talking. Just beside his finger, Doc Holliday stares out from a sticker. Underneath him, two words: “Say when.”

Alan’s contributions aren’t always strictly scientific. He also provides the dad jokes.

Alan Davis 

I want to raise, you know, I deserve more.

Kathryn Martinez 

Which, makes sense.

Dennis Garcia

I don’t know if it’s a joke, but we actually spend more time together than we do our own family, it seems like. and a lot of times I think that’s true.

Kathryn Martinez 

Art agrees.

Art Pardo

We have a good family atmosphere. We have our own family issues sometimes, but we resolve them and we move on and we get the work done. I guess I can be considered a big brother because I’ve been here one of one of the people has been here the longest.

Kathryn Martinez

In this family, everyone does their part.

Daniel Rodriguez

My style is more like leading by example, so I I try to do the best job possible that I can do from my side, so that hopefully other people see that and get inspired to try to do a good job.

Kathryn Martinez 

After spending a day with some of NASA’s brightest minds, I’m feeling pretty inspired myself.

Paola Rodriguez

Can you ask me the question and then I can answer to you because then my brain will-

Kathryn Martinez 

Sitting with Paola, it’s hard to believe that not long ago she wondered whether she even belonged in this strange place she now calls home.

“It can be a little intimidating,” she says. “You can start to question yourself.“

Paola will tell you she’s nothing special.

Paola Rodriguez

No me considero nada especial.

Kathryn Martinez

Which I can tell you flat out isn’t true. You have to be at least a little extraordinary to end up in the White Sands Hypervelocity Lab.

Paola Rodriguez 

Creo que si yo puede los demás pueden ni lo digo con todo el la humildad posible.

Kathryn Martinez 

She says if she can do it, other people can too, which is a lovely thought. I’m not sure it applies to me.

Kathryn Martinez

Thanks for sticking around. I hope you enjoyed this first episode from our team at White Sands.

There’s still more to come in the White Sands series. Stay tuned for our second episode, Beyond the Spark: The Oxygen Team Protecting Spaceflight, coming out next month, December 2026. In the meantime, you can explore more capabilities and stories about White Sands at NASA.gov/White-Sands-Test-Facility.

articles.author: Jillian C. York
articles.title: When the Watchdogs Are Silenced: India's Crackdown on Those Documenting Online Censorship
articles.excerpt: On November 3, our colleagues at the Software Freedom Law Center, India (SFLC.in) received notifications from X that the Delhi Police had issued takedown requests targeting 42 URLs. Among the accounts and posts targeted were those belonging to SFLC.in, the Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF), and X account @geoblockedindia, as well as posts documenting legal notices and instances of online censorship.
articles.content:
Jillian C. York · Electronic Frontier Foundation · CC BY 4.0

On November 3, our colleagues at the Software Freedom Law Center, India (SFLC.in) received notifications from X that the Delhi Police had issued takedown requests targeting 42 URLs. Among the accounts and posts targeted were those belonging to SFLC.in, the Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF), and X account @geoblockedindia, as well as posts documenting legal notices and instances of online censorship. 

Takedown requests targeting SFLC.in and other digital rights groups threaten not only their work, but the public’s ability to know when and how online speech is being restricted. 

The requests cite grounds including hate speech, alleged defamation of the Hindu nationalist organization Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS), and concerns relating to safety and security. But the context in which these requests have emerged is particularly troubling: they target organizations and individuals whose work involves documenting restrictions on online expression and making those restrictions visible to the public. 

In other words, the organizations being targeted are among those trying to tell the public when and how its speech is being censored. 

SFLC.in is one of India's most important digital rights organizations and promotes innovation and open access to knowledge by helping developers make great free and open-source software, protects privacy and civil liberties for Indians by educating and providing free legal advice, and helps policymakers make informed and just decisions about use of technology. In 2025, we recognized their work with an EFF Award for Defending Digital Freedoms. 

IFF (the Internet Freedom Foundation) is another of EFF's close allies in India. Like EFF, IFF combines advocacy campaigns and strategic litigation to advance digital rights. They write frequently about internet shutdowns and have filed several lawsuits contesting them. 

Among SFLC.in's initiatives is its Free Speech Tracker, which documents instances of online censorship, content restrictions, and account takedowns in India. In a country where government orders to restrict online content are often opaque, this work is absolutely essential. 
 
Recent legal notices object to the tracker itself, as well as the organization’s documentation of restricted content and geo-blocked material. The allegations against SFLC.in include claims that it is "continuously opposing government directions" and publicly circulating information about restricted content, thereby undermining measures taken in the name of national security and public order. 

But documenting government censorship is not the same as undermining public safety. Reporting that content has been restricted is not an endorsement of that content, nor does it constitute an attempt to circumvent the law. It is an exercise in transparency and accountability, and one that allows journalists, researchers, civil society organizations, and the public to understand how governments exercise their power over the information landscape. 

Censorship thrives in the absence of transparency 

The use of legal complaints and platform takedown mechanisms against organizations documenting censorship creates a particularly troubling dynamic. When those who monitor restrictions on expression are threatened with having their accounts or reporting removed, the result is a chilling effect that extends far beyond the immediate targets. Other organizations or journalists may think twice before documenting controversial takedowns or challenging government orders, and the public loses access to an independent record of decisions that affect its ability to speak and access information online. 

There is also an important role here for platforms like X. Platforms must be transparent about the requests they receive, provide meaningful notice to affected users, and ensure that any restrictions are subject to appropriate scrutiny and avenues for appeal. When governments seek to restrict speech, platforms have a responsibility to avoid becoming opaque intermediaries through which censorship is quietly carried out. 

These developments are part of a broader pattern of pressure on independent civil society organizations working to defend freedom of expression and access to information in India. Digital rights groups play an indispensable role in documenting the effects of government policies, identifying patterns of censorship, and challenging restrictions that undermine fundamental rights. Their ability to do so independently is not a peripheral concern; it is a cornerstone of a healthy democratic society. 

The right to freedom of expression includes the right to scrutinize the exercise of government power. That includes the right to document censorship, question the reasons given for it, and make that information available to the public.  

EFF stands in solidarity with SFLC.in, the Internet Freedom Foundation, @geoblockedindia, and all those working to document and challenge restrictions on online expression in India. We urge the authorities in India to respect the rights of digital rights organizations to conduct their work without intimidation or retaliation, and to ensure that any restrictions on online expression comply with international human rights standards.
