articles.content:
Home Assistant contributors · Home Assistant · CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

Home Assistant 2026.10! 🎉

Last week, Nabu Casa dropped: Big Tech ruined the cloud, so we’re renaming ours. Home Assistant Cloud is on its way to becoming Home Assistant Link. Same service, new name. I love that title, by the way. If you haven’t read the story behind it yet, go have a look, and tell us what you think. The change is planned for the December release, so there is still time. 🏎️

Now, I’ll let you in on a secret: I’m an automation person. Dashboards are lovely and I admire everyone who builds a pretty one, but for me, automationsAutomations in Home Assistant allow you to automatically respond to things that happen in and around your home. [Learn more] are what make a smart home actually smart. So you can imagine how happy I am with what’s in this release. One of the most powerful features you never thought you’d need has been sitting in Home Assistant for years: trigger IDs. Give your triggersA trigger is the part of an automation that makes the automation start when something specific happens, for example, when the sun sets, a door opens, or a button is pressed. [Learn more] an ID, and one automation can do the job of two, three, or five. It was also tucked away in a menu, you had to invent the IDs yourself, and then remember which was which. Plenty of you never found it, and that’s on us.

Not anymore. Trigger IDs finally get a proper UI: you check the triggers you want in the condition, and Home Assistant takes care of the IDs behind the scenes. And if you like writing your own IDs in YAMLYAML is a human-readable data serialization language. It is used to store and transmit data in a structured format. In Home Assistant, YAML is used for configuration, for example in the configuration.yaml or automations.yaml files. [Learn more], nothing changes. Those keep working exactly as before. That makes it my favorite of this release. 🧠

Don’t get me wrong, the map is absolutely a cool feature too. Last release, every map in Home Assistant broke overnight when our map provider wanted an API key. We moved to OpenStreetMap, and it turns out that swapping out the map opens a lot of doors: a vector map that stays sharp at every zoom level, redesigned markers, and an overview of where everyone has been. You are here. 📍

There’s more: a tidier profile page, a panel for your Modbus connections, connecting your AI in one click, and 15 new integrationsIntegrations connect and integrate Home Assistant with your devices, services, and more. [Learn more]! 🚀

Enjoy the release!

../Frenck

  • Cloud becomes Link
  • A whole new map
    • Crisp at every zoom level
    • Redesigned markers
    • An overview for the Map dashboard
    • Zones on the new map
  • A tidier profile page
  • The best automation feature you never used
  • Integrations
    • New integrations
    • Noteworthy improvements to existing integrations
    • Integration quality scale achievements
    • Now available to set up from the UI
    • Farewell to the following
  • Other noteworthy changes
    • Show a card only when it matters
    • A panel for your Modbus connections
    • Connect your AI in one click
    • Name an entity after its device
    • Timers, one tap away
  • Patch releases
    • 2026.10.1 - October 10
    • 2026.10.2 - October 16
    • 2026.10.3 - October 23
    • 2026.10.4 - October 24
  • Need help? Join the community
  • Backward-incompatible changes
  • All changes

A huge thank you to all the contributors who made this release possible! And a special shout-out to @googanhiem and @piitaya who helped write these release notes. Also, @grischard, @moryoav, and @RaHehl for putting effort into tweaking its contents. Thanks to them, these release notes are in great shape. ❤️

Cloud becomes Link

In case you missed it, we’re making the move to rename Home Assistant Cloud to Home Assistant Link. Same service, new name.

We’re all pretty annoyed by how Big Tech has been ruining perfectly good smart home devices by making them reliant on the cloud. Ours has never locked anyone in, harvested their data, or turned working devices into e-waste, so a new name was in order. Home Assistant Link is all about being clearer that it does things differently. The change is planned for the December release, so tell us your thoughts before then.

The best link is a fast link. 🏎️ Nabu Casa has been hard at work making remote access even faster across the globe. They recently migrated all of their servers to bare metal and added more servers to boost their coverage of the world. This month, they added a latency checker that pings multiple servers on boot and picks the best connection for you.

A whole new map

Last release, something changed underneath every map in Home Assistant, and we barely mentioned it in the release notes. The map provider we relied on started stamping an “API key required” message across its map images, breaking every map in Home Assistant at once. Instead of hunting for another free tile provider, we switched from pre-rendered map images to vector tiles generated and served by the OpenStreetMap Foundation. Both maps use OpenStreetMap data, but your device now draws the map itself. The new Map tiles integration fetches and caches the tiles through your Home Assistant instance, so your browser does not contact external tile servers directly. Recently viewed parts of the map remain available through a short internet hiccup.

Guillaume Rischard (@grischard), the former chair of the OpenStreetMap Foundation who initiated and led its vector-tile initiative, joined us during the 2026.9 release party.

Swapping out the map underneath opened a lot of doors. This release walks through the first few.

Crisp at every zoom level

The map is drawn entirely on your device, as vectors, instead of being stitched together from pictures. Streets and labels stay sharp at any zoom level, and zooming in and out is smooth. The map also has a dedicated dark style, with colors designed for dark mode. Older devices that can’t render vector maps, like the old tablet on your wall, automatically fall back to the classic map.

Redesigned markers

The markers on the map got a complete redesign. People show up with their picture, zonesZones allow you to specify certain regions on a map. They enable zone presence-detection and can be used in automations. For example, to start the vacuum after you left home or start the heating at home when you leave the office. [Learn more] get a marker with their icon in their own color, and everyone in the same zone shares a single bubble on that zone, instead of a pile of markers stacked on top of each other. Zoom out far enough, and bubbles that would overlap merge into one.

An overview for the Map dashboard

The Map dashboard now comes with an overview, next to the map on a desktop and as a sheet you pull up on your phone. It has three tabs: People, Devices, and Zones. Select someone to see their recent activity, with each stop colored by the zone they were in. Select a zone to see who’s there. On a phone, the map now also fills the whole screen, edge to edge.

The same overview shows up when you put a map card in a panel view on your own dashboard.

Zones on the new map

The zone editor in Settings > Areas, labels & zones now uses the same new map. Your zones are sorted alphabetically, with Home always at the top, and they show the same icons and colors you see on the map.

The redesign follows an Open Home Foundation design concept for the Map dashboard.

Thanks to @maartenla, @matthiasdebaat, @bramkragten, and @bgoncal; @grischard for initiating vector maps on the OpenStreetMap side and for assisting us; and Paul Norman (@pnorman) for developing Tilekiln and the tile service. Thanks also to the OpenStreetMap Foundation and the MapLibre, Shortbread, and VersaTiles communities.

Like Home Assistant, OpenStreetMap is built in the open by people like you. Spot something in your neighborhood that’s missing or out of date? You can leave a note or edit the map yourself.

A tidier profile page

Select your name at the bottom of the sidebar, and you land on your User profile. Over the years, that page quietly turned into a bit of a junk drawer. Language, theme, date formats, sidebar order, push notifications, keyboard shortcuts: all stacked in one long General tab, with Security as its only neighbor. Everything was there. You just had to scroll past most of it to find the one thing you came for.

The profile page is now an overview, using the same kind of navigation you already know from Settings. At the top is a card with your account, followed by your Theme, and a short list of sections that each hold a handful of related settings:

  • Appearance: Your default dashboard and the order of your sidebar
  • Localization: Your language, time zone, and how dates, times, and numbers are shown
  • This browser (or This mobile app in the companion app): Notifications, display, and shortcuts for the device you’re using right now
  • Security: Your password, multi-factor authentication, and access tokens

Nothing was taken away. Every setting is still there, just grouped so it’s easier to find. Thanks, @pcan08 and @maartenla!

That account card at the top learned a new trick, too. Until now, your own name and picture weren’t actually yours to change. Only an administrator could set them, tucked away in the person settings. Not an administrator, but you wanted a nicer picture of yourself in the sidebar? You had to go ask whoever runs your Home Assistant. A bit odd, for something that is literally your face.

Every user, administrator or not, now has an Edit profile button right next to Log out. Upload and crop a picture, change your name, and save. Your name is used for both your user and the person linked to it, so it’s the same everywhere you show up, from the sidebar to your dashboards and Assist. Your new picture shows up in the sidebar right away.

The best automation feature you never used

Take a look at your automationsAutomations in Home Assistant allow you to automatically respond to things that happen in and around your home. [Learn more], and chances are you’ll find a few that come in pairs. One turns the hallway light on when motion is detected, the other turns it off again when the motion stops. One sends a notification when the washing machine starts, the other when it’s done. Two automations, doing one job.

Home Assistant has had a way to combine those into one for years. Give each triggerA trigger is the part of an automation that makes the automation start when something specific happens, for example, when the sun sets, a door opens, or a button is pressed. [Learn more] an ID, and use the Triggered by conditionConditions check whether something is true at that moment, for example, whether a door is closed. You can use them in automations and scripts. If a condition is not met, the actions that come after it in the same sequence do not run. At the top level of an automation or script, this stops the automation or script. [Learn more] to do something different depending on which trigger fired. It’s one of the most powerful things you can do in the automation editor, and also one of the best-hidden. The trigger ID field sat in the menu of each trigger. You had to come up with an ID, type it in yourself, and then remember which ID belonged to which trigger when you picked them in the condition. Most people never found it, and honestly, we can’t blame them.

Not anymore. Add a Triggered by condition, and you check the triggers it should match. You see the triggers themselves, not some ID you made up, and each one is numbered by its position in your list, with the same number shown next to the trigger itself. So you always know which one is which. There are no IDs to come up with at all. Home Assistant takes care of those behind the scenes, and cleans up after itself when you remove a trigger.

If you set your trigger IDs yourself in YAMLYAML is a human-readable data serialization language. It is used to store and transmit data in a structured format. In Home Assistant, YAML is used for configuration, for example in the configuration.yaml or automations.yaml files. [Learn more], nothing changes. Those IDs keep working exactly as they did, sharing one ID between several triggers is still fine, and Home Assistant won’t add IDs to your YAML for you. The trigger ID field is gone from the automation editor, because you no longer need it there: to run the same actions for several triggers, check them all in one Triggered by condition.

The editor does keep an eye out for two things, but only in the Triggered by condition. If a condition points to a trigger that no longer exists, it flags it, so you can clear it. And if several triggers share the same ID, it shows a warning with a Fix that gives each trigger its own ID and updates your conditions to match. It’s a suggestion, not a repair, so if sharing an ID is what you want, you can leave it as it is.

This completes an Open Home Foundation roadmap opportunity to make referencing triggers in automations a lot easier. Thanks, @jpbede, @wendevlin, @marcinbauer-ohf, and @nielsrowinbik!

While you’re in the automation editor, you’ll notice your triggersA trigger is the part of an automation that makes the automation start when something specific happens, for example, when the sun sets, a door opens, or a button is pressed. [Learn more], conditionsConditions check whether something is true at that moment, for example, whether a door is closed. You can use them in automations and scripts. If a condition is not met, the actions that come after it in the same sequence do not run. At the top level of an automation or script, this stops the automation or script. [Learn more], and actionsAn action makes Home Assistant do something, for example, turn on a light, send a notification, or activate a scene. Automations and scripts run a list of actions. [Learn more] tell you a bit more at a glance. Each row now shows the details that used to be hidden until you opened it: the threshold a trigger or condition checks for, like “above 10 °C”, how long something needs to stay that way, the offset on a sunrise or sunset, and how long a wait action waits before it gives up. Thanks, @wendevlin and @MindFreeze!

Integrations

Thanks to our community for keeping pace with the new integrationsIntegrations connect and integrate Home Assistant with your devices, services, and more. [Learn more] and improvements to existing ones! You’re all awesome 🥰

New integrations

We welcome the following new integrations in this release:

  • Axle Energy, added by @Herbertmt978
    Bring the grid event schedule of your Axle Energy account into Home Assistant. It tells you whether an upcoming event asks you to import from or export to the grid, and exactly when it starts and ends, so your automationsAutomations in Home Assistant allow you to automatically respond to things that happen in and around your home. [Learn more] can get your home ready in time.

  • Bitvis Power Hub, added by @MandusBorjesson
    Read real-time electricity data from your smart meter using a Bitvis Power Hub, which plugs into the meter’s HAN port. The Power Hub pushes its measurements, like power, voltage, and current per phase, straight to Home Assistant over your local network. No cloud, no pollingData polling is the process of querying a device or service at regular intervals to check for updates or retrieve data. By defining a custom polling interval, you can control how frequently your system checks for new data, which can help optimize performance and reduce unnecessary network traffic. [Learn more].

  • Gree Infrared, added by @Dr-Blank, launching at 🥈 silver quality
    Control a Gree air conditioner using any infrared transmitter you already have set up in Home Assistant, like an ESPHome device with an infrared LED. Add an infrared receiver, and the climateThe Climate entity allows you to control and monitor HVAC (heating, ventilating, and air conditioning) devices and thermostats. [Learn more] entity follows along when someone uses the physical Gree remote. Gree builds air conditioners for many brands, so units sold as Onida, Sinclair, and others work as well.

  • INDI Allsky, added by @TN-1
    Connect your INDI Allsky camera server, an allsky camera system for astrophotography and keeping an eye on cloud cover. You get the latest capture as a camera, plus sensors for sky quality, the number of stars detected, exposure time, and whether it’s night.

  • KACO Modbus, added by @g4bri3lDev
    Connect a KACO new energy solar inverter directly over your local network using Modbus TCP. It shows what the inverter is producing right now, its lifetime energy counter for the Energy dashboard, and what it is doing, without any cloud account or manufacturer portal involved.

  • my-PV, added by @rrooggiieerr
    Control my-PV devices, like the AC•THOR range and AC ELWA 2, which turn your surplus solar power into hot water. Home Assistant talks to them locally and discovers them on your network automatically.

  • OSRAM Infrared, added by @freeDom-, launching at 🥈 silver quality
    Control OSRAM and LEDVANCE RGB lights that come with a 24-button infrared remote, using an infrared transmitter set up in Home Assistant. With an infrared receiver, the lightA light has a brightness you can control, and optionally color temperature or RGB color control. [Learn more] entity also picks up commands from the physical remote.

  • Persang Infrared, added by @Dr-Blank
    Control a Persang Bluetooth speaker using an infrared transmitter set up in Home Assistant, giving you a media player and buttons for its remote functions.

  • SolarEdge Modbus, added by @frenck, launching at 🏆 platinum quality
    Connect to your SolarEdge solar inverter over your own network, using the Modbus TCP interface built into the inverter. No account, no API key, no cloud. Readings arrive every few seconds instead of every few minutes, and keep arriving when your internet connection is down. You can also change the export limit and how your battery charges.

  • Sunsynk, added by @jamesridgway
    Bring your Sunsynk hybrid solar inverter and battery into Home Assistant using your Sunsynk Connect account. You get sensors for solar production, grid import and export, and your battery. Home Assistant can even discover the Sunsynk data logger on your network.

  • Theben Conexa Smart Meter Gateway, added by @mdluhosch
    Read your meter data locally from a Theben Conexa 3.0 smart meter gateway, using its built-in Home Area Network (HAN) interface. No cloud needed.

  • Threema, added by @LukasQ
    Send end-to-end encrypted messages from your automationsAutomations in Home Assistant allow you to automatically respond to things that happen in and around your home. [Learn more] to people on Threema, the privacy-focused messenger that doesn’t need a phone number. It uses the Threema Gateway service, and each person you add as a recipient gets their own notify entity.

  • Vitesy, added by @chemelli74
    Connect the Vitesy Shelfy, an air purifier that lives in your refrigerator. See the air quality and temperature inside your fridge, how often the door was opened, and when the filter needs cleaning or replacing. You can even switch the purifier mode, for example to boost it after a grocery run.

  • Willow, added by @PaxPrz
    Keep an eye on the health of your indoor plants with Willow sensors. Temperature, humidity, soil moisture, and light levels come from the Willow cloud into Home Assistant, ready for your dashboards and automationsAutomations in Home Assistant allow you to automatically respond to things that happen in and around your home. [Learn more]. Your plants can’t tell you they’re thirsty, but now Home Assistant can.

  • Zonneplan, added by @erwindouna
    Get the electricity and gas prices of your Zonneplan contract, a Dutch provider of dynamic energy contracts. Handy for running your appliances when energy is cheapest.

This release also has new virtual integrations. Virtual integrations are stubs that are handled by other (existing) integrations to help with findability. These ones are new:

  • Austroflamm, provided by Fumis, added by @frenck
  • EcoSpar, provided by Fumis, added by @frenck
  • HAAS+SOHN, provided by Fumis, added by @frenck
  • HETA, provided by Fumis, added by @frenck
  • O General, provided by FGLair, added by @Dr-Blank
  • Onida Infrared, provided by Gree Infrared, added by @Dr-Blank
  • Steinway & Lyngdorf, provided by Lyngdorf, added by @fishloa

Noteworthy improvements to existing integrations

It is not just new integrationsIntegrations connect and integrate Home Assistant with your devices, services, and more. [Learn more] that have been added; existing ones keep getting better too. Here are some of the noteworthy improvements this release:

  • Matter added switchesSwitches are things that have two states you can select between, such as turning on or off a socket. [Learn more] to turn the visual and audible alarms of supported leak sensors on or off, like the IKEA KLIPPBOK, and a switch for one-touch locking, so you decide whether a single touch on the keypad of your lock is enough to lock the door. DevicesA device is a model representing a physical or logical unit that contains entities. that measure electrical power now also report the frequency and power factor. Thanks, @wardmatter, @mmmspatz, and @lboue!
  • Tuya supports a lot more devicesA device is a model representing a physical or logical unit that contains entities. this release: two-channel DIN rail energy meters with readings per channel, circuit breakers, EV chargers (with their charging current, charging mode, and session energy), water valves (with water usage and temperature), and the keypad tone and alarm push settings of the Duosmart C30 alarm panel. Three-phase electricity meters now also report reactive power, apparent power, and power factor for each phase. Thanks, @keranm, @tmunzer, @o-borovets, @syl-craft, @ChayoteJarocho, @huangrenwei79, and @epenet!
  • Internet Printing Protocol (IPP) added page counters, so you can keep track of how many pages, impressions, and sheets your printer has gone through, split into color and black and white on printers that report it. Thanks, @brianegge!
  • ESPHome devicesA device is a model representing a physical or logical unit that contains entities. can now open the connection to Home Assistant themselves, so they work even when Home Assistant can’t reach them directly. Turn on the outgoing_connection option on your ESPHome device, and Home Assistant takes it from there, with the same encryption as always. Thanks, @bdraco!
  • HomeKit Bridge can now show your valve entitiesAn entity represents a sensor, actor, or function in Home Assistant. Entities are used to monitor physical properties or to control other entities. An entity is usually part of a device or a service. [Learn more] in the Home app as a faucet, shower head, or sprinkler. How long a valve runs can now also come from any number entity, not just a number helperA helper is a virtual entity you create inside Home Assistant. It is not backed by a physical device. Helpers store values, track state, or do calculations that your automations and dashboards need. [Learn more]. Thanks, @louwii17!
  • Philips Hue added a switch to turn each MotionAware zone on or off, just like you can in the Hue app. Rooms and zones also gained a sceneScenes capture the states you want certain entities to be. For example, a scene can specify that light A should be turned on and light B should be bright red. [Learn more] select, showing which scene (or smart scene) is currently active, and letting you pick another one. Thanks, @marcelveldt and @sliekens!
  • Reolink can now control the pan and tilt lens of cameras that combine multiple lenses in one device, when connected to a Reolink NVR or Home Hub. Thanks, @starkillerOG!
  • Music Assistant announcements can now speak a message, not only play an audio file. The announcement action takes a message and a “text-to-speech”TTS (text-to-speech) allows Home Assistant to talk to you. [Learn more] entity to speak it, while keeping the pre-announcement chime and announcement volume that tts.speak doesn’t offer. Farewell to the following

Time for a little cleaning, and no, we did not wait for spring! The following “integrations”Integrations connect and integrate Home Assistant with your devices, services, and more. [Learn more] are no longer available as of this release:

  • Dublin Bus has been removed. It relied on the Real-Time Passenger Information API, which the National Transport Authority shut down in September 2020, so it has not worked since. For scheduled departures, the GTFS integration can use the timetable data published by Transport for Ireland.
  • Etherscan has been removed. It relied on version 1 of the Etherscan API, which has been shut down, so its sensors only showed False instead of a balance. To keep tracking a wallet balance, you can use the RESTful sensor with the Etherscan V2 API and your own free API key.
  • Melnor RainCloud has been removed. Melnor discontinued the original RainCloud WiFi Timer in April 2026, and its cloud service no longer responds.
  • Orange and Rockland Utility (ORU) has been removed. The endpoint it relied on stopped returning meter data years ago. Orange and Rockland customers can use the Opower integration instead.
  • Sigfox has been removed. It relied on version 1 of the Sigfox backend API, which Sigfox retired.
  • SolarEdge Local has been removed. It relied on a local web API that SolarEdge disabled in inverter firmware updates starting in 2020. Use the SolarEdge integration, or the new SolarEdge Modbus integration if you want to keep things local.
  • Travis-CI has been removed. It relied on the travis-ci.org API, which Travis CI shut down in June 2021.
  • Zestimate has been removed. Zillow retired the API it relied on, and its replacement is aimed at commercial use, so the integration could not simply be updated.

Connect your AI in one click

Home Assistant can act as a Model Context Protocol server, which lets AI apps like Claude, ChatGPT, or Cursor talk to your home. Getting there was a bit of a hunt, though: add the integrationIntegrations connect and integrate Home Assistant with your devices, services, and more. [Learn more], pick which parts of Home Assistant to expose, and then figure out which URL to hand to your AI app.

The AI tasks page under Settings > System is now called AI, and it gained a Model Context Protocol card. Turn the server on in a single click, and the card lists the URLs to paste into your AI app, each with a button to copy it. New setups expose everything Home Assistant has to offer, including anything added later, and only allow administrator accounts to connect. You can change both whenever you like, without removing and re-adding the integration.

It also works the other way around. Apps that run their own MCP server are now discovered automatically by the Model Context Protocol integration, so connecting Home Assistant to them only takes a confirmation.

And your AI got a lot better at finding music. Ask it to play something, and instead of blindly playing the first search result, it now gets a list of results and picks the best match. It can even search inside an artist, album, or playlist to find that one specific song. Search itself improved along the way: artists, albums, and playlists from Music Assistant can now be searched inside, just like results from Jellyfin and Squeezebox, local media now finds matching folders too, and Radio Browser puts the 100 most popular stations first.

Thanks, @balloob!

If your home runs on KNX, your AI can now dig into that too. The KNX integration brings its own set of AI tools, which you can hand to your conversation agent, or to your AI app through the Model Context Protocol server. Ask about the group addresses, devices, and functions in your ETS project, go through the history of telegrams on your bus, or decode a value you don’t recognize. It can even read and write values on the bus directly. Thanks, @martinhoefling!

Need help? Join the community

Home Assistant has a great community of users who are all more than willing to help each other out. So, join us!

Our very active Discord chat server is an excellent place to be, and don’t forget to join our amazing forums.

Found a bug or issue? Please report it in our issue tracker to get it fixed! Or check our help page for guidance on more places you can go.

Are you more into email? Sign up for the Open Home Foundation Newsletter to get the latest news about features, things happening in our community, and other projects that support the Open Home straight into your inbox.

Backward-incompatible changes

We do our best to avoid making changes to existing functionality that might unexpectedly impact your Home Assistant installation. Unfortunately, sometimes it is inevitable.

We always make sure to document these changes to make the transition as easy as possible for you. This release has the following backward-incompatible changes:

Authentication

The deprecated legacy mode of the Home Assistant authentication provider has been removed. Usernames are now always handled in their normalized form: lowercase, and without spaces at the start or end. If Home Assistant showed you a repair about usernames that are not normalized, change those usernames to match.

(@gjohansson-ST - #175613) (Authentication documentation)

easyEnergy

The hours_priced_equal_or_lower and hours_priced_equal_or_higher sensors are now named Periods priced equal or lower and Periods priced equal or higher, and no longer have h as their unit of measurement. Their values count price periods, not hours.

If you have “templates”A template is an automation definition that can include variables for the action or data from the trigger values. This allows automations to generate dynamic actions. [Learn more] or dashboard cards that rely on the unit of these sensors, update them to handle a count without a unit. The values, entity IDs, and unique IDs are unchanged, so automationsAutomations in Home Assistant allow you to automatically respond to things that happen in and around your home. [Learn more] that only compare the numbers need no changes.

(@klaasnicolaas - #181431) (easyEnergy documentation)

EnergyFlip

EnergyFlip shut down the API version the integration used, so the integration has moved to the new version. The new API no longer provides the additional electricity measurements, so only the current power sensor remains for electricity.

(@DieEneSchrodinger - #179723) (EnergyFlip documentation)

EnergyZero

The hours_priced_equal_or_lower electricity sensor is now named Periods priced equal or lower, and no longer has h as its unit of measurement. Its value counts price periods, not hours.

If you have “templates”A template is an automation definition that can include variables for the action or data from the trigger values. This allows automations to generate dynamic actions. [Learn more] or dashboard cards that rely on the unit of this sensor, update them to handle a count without a unit. The value, entity ID, and unique ID are unchanged, so automationsAutomations in Home Assistant allow you to automatically respond to things that happen in and around your home. [Learn more] that only compare the number need no changes.

(@klaasnicolaas - #181492) (EnergyZero documentation)

Google Sheets

Reading an empty worksheet now returns {"range": [[]]} instead of {"range": []}. If you have automationsAutomations in Home Assistant allow you to automatically respond to things that happen in and around your home. [Learn more], scriptsA script is a saved list of steps that runs when you start it, for example, from a dashboard, with Assist, or from an automation. Unlike an automation, a script has no triggers, so it doesn’t start by itself. [Learn more], or “templates”A template is an automation definition that can include variables for the action or data from the trigger values. This allows automations to generate dynamic actions. [Learn more] that check for an empty worksheet, update them to match.

(@JamieMagee - #181692) (Google Sheets documentation)

Google Wifi

The uptime sensor is deprecated and will be removed in a future release. Use the new last restart sensor instead.

(@EReaso - #177525) (Google Wifi documentation)

IoTaWatt

Reactive power sensors now use the reactive power device class, which changes their unit of measurement from VAR to var. You have these sensors if an output on your IoTaWatt is configured with the unit VAR.

If such a sensor has recorded long-term statisticsHome Assistant keeps statistics for sensors that have a state class, such as measurement, total, or total increasing. Every 5 minutes, it saves short-term statistics, which are deleted after 10 days by default. Every hour, it saves long-term statistics, which are never deleted automatically. The Energy dashboard and statistics cards use them. [Learn more], Home Assistant creates a repair about the changed unit after the update. Pick the offered option to update the statistics to the new unit. No data is lost. In return, these sensors are now shown as reactive power, and you can display them in mvar, var, or kvar.

(@agners - #180913) (IoTaWatt documentation)

Libre Hardware Monitor

Libre Hardware Monitor versions older than 0.9.5 are no longer supported. If you run an older version, update Libre Hardware Monitor to keep using the integration.

(@Sab44 - #181928) (Libre Hardware Monitor documentation)

Linode and Tank Utility

The Linode and Tank Utility integrationsIntegrations connect and integrate Home Assistant with your devices, services, and more. [Learn more] have been disabled and no longer start.

Both depend on Python libraries that have not been maintained for years (the Linode one was last updated in 2018, the Tank Utility one in 2023) and no longer work with current Python packaging tools. Keeping them running meant holding back those tools for every other integration, so they have been switched off instead.

If you use either integration, you can remove it from your configuration. If the underlying libraries are updated, or replaced with maintained alternatives, the integrations can be activated again. Community contributions to make this happen are very welcome.

(@frenck - #182842) (Linode documentation) (Tank Utility documentation)

Mealie

Mealie 3.2 or newer is now required. Version 3.2 was released in September 2025, and the Mealie appApps are additional standalone third-party software packages that can be installed on Home Assistant OS. [Learn more] and official container are already well past it, so most of you don’t need to do anything. If your Mealie server runs an older version, update it before you update Home Assistant.

(@andrew-codechimp - #180609) (Mealie documentation)

MQTT

The mqtt.publish and mqtt.dump actions now require an administrator account, just like mqtt.reload already did.

AutomationsAutomations in Home Assistant allow you to automatically respond to things that happen in and around your home. [Learn more], scriptsA script is a saved list of steps that runs when you start it, for example, from a dashboard, with Assist, or from an automation. Unlike an automation, a script has no triggers, so it doesn’t start by itself. [Learn more], and scenesScenes capture the states you want certain entities to be. For example, a scene can specify that light A should be turned on and light B should be bright red. [Learn more] that publish on their own are not affected, because they run without a user context. What changes is a call a non-admin user makes themselves: from a dashboard button, from the developer tools, or by starting a script or automation by hand. Those now fail with “Unauthorized”. If a non-admin user needs to be able to publish, let the automation run on its own trigger instead of having that user start it.

(@frenck - #182045) (MQTT documentation)

OpenEVSE

The Charging status sensor now reports a fixed set of states in snake_case, such as charging, not_connected, and gfci_self_test_failure, instead of the raw values from the charger, such as Charging or not connected. If you have automationsAutomations in Home Assistant allow you to automatically respond to things that happen in and around your home. [Learn more] or scriptsA script is a saved list of steps that runs when you start it, for example, from a dashboard, with Assist, or from an automation. Unlike an automation, a script has no triggers, so it doesn’t start by itself. [Learn more] that check for the old values, update them to match the new ones.

(@firstof9 - #180329) (OpenEVSE documentation)

Proxmox VE

The Uptime sensor of nodes, virtual machines, and containers now shows a timestamp of when it started, instead of the time since it started in seconds. If you have automationsAutomations in Home Assistant allow you to automatically respond to things that happen in and around your home. [Learn more], scriptsA script is a saved list of steps that runs when you start it, for example, from a dashboard, with Assist, or from an automation. Unlike an automation, a script has no triggers, so it doesn’t start by itself. [Learn more], or “templates”A template is an automation definition that can include variables for the action or data from the trigger values. This allows automations to generate dynamic actions. [Learn more] that use the number of seconds, update them to work with the timestamp.

(@erwindouna - #169704) (Proxmox VE documentation)

Rejseplanen

Rejseplanen now uses version 2.0 of the Rejseplanen API, which requires an API key. You can apply for an API key with Rejseplanen Labs. The integration is now set up from the UI instead of YAMLYAML is a human-readable data serialization language. It is used to store and transmit data in a structured format. In Home Assistant, YAML is used for configuration, for example in the configuration.yaml or automations.yaml files. [Learn more].

All extra attributes have been removed from the sensors. If you have “templates”A template is an automation definition that can include variables for the action or data from the trigger values. This allows automations to generate dynamic actions. [Learn more] or dashboard cards that use them, you need to update them.

(@Jawar19 - #152200) (Rejseplanen documentation)

Sofar

Sofar inverters that report no energy meter no longer get these six energy sensors: Load consumption today, Load consumption total, Import energy today, Import energy total, Export energy today, and Export energy total.

They never held real readings on those inverters. The inverter itself marks those values as invalid, and on a PV-only inverter, Load consumption total simply repeated the solar generation total. If you used these sensors on your Energy dashboard, or in “templates”A template is an automation definition that can include variables for the action or data from the trigger values. This allows automations to generate dynamic actions. [Learn more] or automationsAutomations in Home Assistant allow you to automatically respond to things that happen in and around your home. [Learn more], remove them. Hybrid inverters and PV inverters with a meter keep all six.

(@darkrain-nl - #181729) (Sofar documentation)

State conditions

State conditionsConditions check whether something is true at that moment, for example, whether a door is closed. You can use them in automations and scripts. If a condition is not met, the actions that come after it in the same sequence do not run. At the top level of an automation or script, this stops the automation or script. [Learn more] that combine the for option with a state attribute, a list of states, or a state taken from another entity now fail validation. These combinations don’t support a duration, so you get an error when the configuration is checked, instead of a condition that doesn’t do what you expect.

(@emontnemery - #174083)

Synology DSM

The synology_dsm.reboot and synology_dsm.shutdown actions now require an administrator account.

AutomationsAutomations in Home Assistant allow you to automatically respond to things that happen in and around your home. [Learn more] and scriptsA script is a saved list of steps that runs when you start it, for example, from a dashboard, with Assist, or from an automation. Unlike an automation, a script has no triggers, so it doesn’t start by itself. [Learn more] that run on their own triggers are not affected, because they run without a user context. What changes is a call a non-admin user makes themselves: from a dashboard button, from the developer tools, or by starting a script or automation by hand. Those now fail with “Unauthorized”. If a non-admin user needs to be able to restart or shut down the NAS, let the automation run on its own trigger instead of having that user start it.

(@frenck - #182050) (Synology DSM documentation)

Telegram bot

When you pass a directory_path to the telegram_bot.download_file action, that directory now has to be in your allowlist_external_dirs. If the action starts failing, add the directory to your configuration:

homeassistant:
  allowlist_external_dirs:
    - /media/telegram

If you leave out directory_path, nothing changes. Files are still saved to the telegram_bot folder in your configuration directory, without an allowlist entry.

(@frenck - #182460) (Telegram bot documentation)

Teslemetry

Vehicles that stream their data no longer get the entitiesAn entity represents a sensor, actor, or function in Home Assistant. Entities are used to monitor physical properties or to control other entities. An entity is usually part of a device or a service. [Learn more] that can only be updated by pollingData polling is the process of querying a device or service at regular intervals to check for updates or retrieve data. By defining a custom polling interval, you can control how frequently your system checks for new data, which can help optimize performance and reduce unnecessary network traffic. [Learn more]. Updating those required a paid API call, which most people did not expect.

(@Bre77 - #181351) (Teslemetry documentation)

UniFi Network

You can no longer reconfigure the UniFi Network integrationIntegrations connect and integrate Home Assistant with your devices, services, and more. [Learn more] by adding the same site again through Add integration. Use the dedicated Reconfigure option of the integration instead.

(@robinsiep - #182201) (UniFi Network documentation)

UpCloud

The option to configure the pollingData polling is the process of querying a device or service at regular intervals to check for updates or retrieve data. By defining a custom polling interval, you can control how frequently your system checks for new data, which can help optimize performance and reduce unnecessary network traffic. [Learn more] interval has been removed from UpCloud. The integration now always polls every 60 seconds. If you had set a longer interval, this means more API calls: a 300 second interval, for example, becomes five times as many calls.

If you need a different update frequency, you can set your own polling interval.

(@KingLizard1020 - #181327) (UpCloud documentation)

Xbox

The Subscribed to Xbox Game Pass binary sensorA binary sensor is an entity that reports one of two mutually exclusive states, on or off. The device class determines how those states are labeled in the UI. For example, open/closed for a door or detected/clear for motion. [Learn more] has been removed, because it never worked. The Xbox API always reported false, whether you or your friends were subscribed to Game Pass or not.

(@tr4nt0r - #182734) (Xbox documentation)

If you are a custom integration developer and want to learn about changes and new features available for your integration: Be sure to follow our developer blog. The following changes are the most notable for this release:

  • DeviceEntry.config_entries deprecation is now enforced
  • Deprecating modbus.get_hub in favor of async_get_unit
  • LLM tools return a ToolResult and declare their integration
  • New device and state class selectors
  • New stop action and idle activity for lawn mowers
  • OAuth2 error handling moved into the helper
  • Probatio is our validation engine
  • Shared config flow abort reasons are translated centrally
  • Use Config Entry exceptions in integration migration method

All changes

Of course, there is a lot more in this release. You can find a list of all changes made here: Full changelog for Home Assistant Core 2026.10.

articles.excerpt: Prepare to be dazzled, because this month LEDVANCE join the Works with Home Assistant program as our newest partners 🎉 And what’s more, they bring a huge lineup of certified devices (116, to be exact!) to our community, which means plenty of new ways to light up your home 💡
articles.content:
Home Assistant contributors · Home Assistant · CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

Prepare to be dazzled, because this month LEDVANCE join the Works with Home Assistant program as our newest partners 🎉 And what’s more, they bring a huge lineup of certified devices (116, to be exact!) to our community, which means plenty of new ways to light up your home 💡

A century of bright ideas

We love welcoming established brands as much as newer names to the Works with Home Assistant program, and LEDVANCE are… well… both! The company was created in 2016 when OSRAM, one of the lighting industry’s oldest and most respected names, spun off its general lighting business as an independent entity. Its name combines “LED” and “advance,” a nod to the shift toward modern LED lighting and the possibilities that came with it.

Since then, LEDVANCE have grown into a global name in their own right, with offices in more than 50 countries and customers in more than 140. They carry forward more than 100 years of lighting experience, and still sell products under the OSRAM brand through a licensing agreement.

But while their heritage is strong, their focus is firmly on the future. Their OSRAM SMART+ range brings that expertise into the modern smart home (and now our program 🎉), embracing Matter to give you more freedom to illuminate your environment around the way you live. With so many devices to choose from, whatever you’re picturing for your home, chances are there’s a LEDVANCE light that can help you make it happen.

Setting the standard

Every LEDVANCE device certified to the program uses Matter with a Wi-Fi connection, making the devices simple to integrate into your existing setup. For any newcomers, Matter is an open standard developed by the Connectivity Standards Alliance. It lets devices from different brands work together locally, so you’re never locked into one company’s ecosystem and your data stays where it should be – in your home.

Since LEDVANCE’s Matter devices use Wi-Fi, you won’t need any extra gear to get started. Just add them to your network and they’ll talk to Home Assistant directly, ensuring an easy setup and the option to create automations with the devices you already have. It’s great to see our new partners prioritizing open standards, showing they care as much as we do about helping our community control their smart homes on their own terms.

“We believe that openness and interoperability are essential for the future of smart homes. By joining the Home Assistant community, we want to make SMART+ products more accessible to users who value flexibility and local control, while learning from the community and collaborating to create better smart home experiences.”

– Pulkit Dhanuka, Product Manager at LEDVANCE

Devices

LEDVANCE’s certified devices cover everything from filament-style bulbs, spotlights, and recessed and track downlights, to ceiling and wall lights, floor lamps, and flexible LED strips for adding a glow under kitchen cabinets or behind the TV. In fact, there are so many options that the list is too long to include in this blog, so head to the certified device list to check out all the details!

Set the scene for a comfy night in with LEDVANCE’s smart lights.

To give you a snapshot, most of the range is tunable white or full color, so your lights can go from a cozy evening glow to crisp morning brightness (or a full rainbow, if the mood strikes). There are also IP-rated options for bathrooms and the garden, including floodlights and outdoor spots, so you can automate your lights beyond the back door, for example to turn your security lights on when a sensor detects motion. And if you prefer to use what you already have, the SMART+ Plug can turn any ordinary lamp or appliance into something you can automate, while smart wall switches do the same for your ceiling lights: replace the switch on the wall, keep the bulbs you have.

As with every device certified to the program, LEDVANCE’s products have been rigorously tested by our in-house team to make sure they comply with our core requirements of local control and privacy. LEDVANCE have also committed to providing long-term support for our community, so you can be confident your setup will keep working for the long run.

Lighting that lasts

Sustainability is one of the core principles of the Open Home Foundation, the non-profit organization that runs Works with Home Assistant. A big part of that is making sure devices stay useful for as long as possible. Since LEDVANCE’s devices don’t need a cloud service to function, you don’t have to worry about a far-off server shutdown turning your lights into e-waste.

And because Matter works across platforms, you’ll still be able to use your tech if you ever change smart home systems. Lighting that keeps shining whatever happens to a platform: that’s the kind of partner we love to welcome, and it’s what this program is all about.

All systems glow

We’re thrilled to have LEDVANCE join our community, and can’t wait to see what you light up with their range of devices. Want to see more partners like them on board? A Home Assistant Link (formerly Home Assistant Cloud) subscription gives you secure, remote access to your smart home, and directly supports the Open Home Foundation to expand our program. Because the more brands that join, the more choice you have to design your space exactly the way you like. Here’s to plenty more switched-on homes 💡 Welcome, LEDVANCE!

FAQs

Q: If I have a device that is not listed under Works with Home Assistant does this mean it’s not supported?

A: No! It just means that it hasn’t gone through a testing schedule with our team or doesn’t fit the requirements of the program. It might function perfectly well but be added to the testing schedule later down the road, or it might work under a different connectivity type that we don’t currently test under the program.

Q: OK, so what’s the point of the Works with program?

A: It highlights the devices we know work well with Home Assistant and the brands that make a long-term commitment to keeping support for these devices going. The certification agreement specifies that the devices must have the functionality you would expect within Home Assistant, operate locally without the need for cloud and that they will continue to do so long-term.

Q: How were these devices tested?

A: All of LEDVANCE’s certified devices were tested using Home Assistant over a standard Wi-Fi connection with our certified Matter integration. If you have another setup or integration that’s not a problem, but we test this way as it’s the most effective method for our team to certify within our ecosystem.

Q: Will you be adding more LEDVANCE devices to the program?

A: Why not! We’re thrilled to foster a close relationship with the team at LEDVANCE to work together on any upcoming releases or add in further products that are not yet listed here.

articles.excerpt: We’re detecting a new presence in the Works with Home Assistant program… and we’re pretty excited about it! A big welcome to our newest partner, Everything Smart Home 🎉 Founded by long-term community member Lewis Barclay and his dad, Dave Barclay, the family-run business brings the Everything Presence line of sensors to the program: the Lite, One, and Pro. All built on ESPHome and designed to keep your data fully local and under your control.
articles.content:
Home Assistant contributors · Home Assistant · CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

We’re detecting a new presence in the Works with Home Assistant program… and we’re pretty excited about it! A big welcome to our newest partner, Everything Smart Home 🎉 Founded by long-term community member Lewis Barclay and his dad, Dave Barclay, the family-run business brings the Everything Presence line of sensors to the program: the Lite, One, and Pro. All built on ESPHome and designed to keep your data fully local and under your control.

A community sensation

If your smart home journey has involved a YouTube rabbit hole or two, chances are you’ve come across Everything Smart Home. And if not, allow us to introduce you! UK-based Lewis created the YouTube channel in 2020. Since then, he’s built a solid reputation in our community and beyond by posting monthly recaps of Home Assistant releases, along with plenty of tips, tricks, and guides on all things home automation.

Lewis’s videos were such a hit with Home Assistant DIYers and enthusiasts that in 2022 Everything Smart Home became one of the first members of our Home Assistant Creator Network. That same year, Lewis and Dave, an electrical engineer, launched Everything Smart Technology to sell smart home gear they believe in (including official Home Assistant hardware from Nabu Casa!). But they didn’t stop there. Lewis also wanted to create devices he’d use in his own home, ones with features he couldn’t find elsewhere. And so the Everything Presence sensor range was born ⚒️

Made ESPecially for you

All three Everything Presence sensors run ESPHome, which lets them talk to Home Assistant directly over your home network, with no cloud connection required. They also carry the Made for ESPHome badge: our guarantee that each device runs ESPHome out of the box, can be fully controlled without opening the case or soldering anything, and has its code made available for all to see.

Everything Smart Home take this responsibility to heart. Their GitHub is a true collective project where users suggest fixes, add features, and find inspiration for sensors of their own. And that commitment goes beyond code: Lewis even joined us at our Open Home Foundation Summit in Dublin last year to discuss what community members want from their tech. We love to see a partner build so openly for our community, and dedicate their time to keeping smart homes local and built to last.

“Home Assistant has been a huge part of our journey from day one, so joining the Works with Home Assistant program with our Everything Presence sensors feels like a natural next step. The Home Assistant community has been incredibly supportive of me ever since pressing publish on that very first video, and we’re incredibly proud to be part of a program that shares our commitment to open, local smart home tech that puts control (and privacy!) firmly in the hands of users.”

— Lewis Barclay, Everything Smart Home

Devices

Like every certified device in the program, the Everything Presence Lite, One, and Pro were tested by our in-house team for local control, privacy, and sustainability, and Everything Smart Home are dedicated to providing long-term support and firmware updates for all three. It’s a commitment that comes naturally: Lewis has plenty of experience using his YouTube channel to listen to users and improve the sensors based on their feedback, so we’ve no doubt the team will continue to bring that same care to our community.

A sensor for every situation: the Everything Presence Lite, One, and Pro (left to right)

So, what makes an Everything Presence sensor different from the motion sensor you might already have? Most motion sensors rely on passive infrared (PIR) alone, so if you sit still long enough, they assume you’ve left (cue: waving at the ceiling). Each Everything Presence sensor uses millimeter-wave (mmWave) radar, which picks up movements as small as breathing, and the One and Pro pair it with PIR for an instant response the moment you walk in. That means lights that stay on while you read, heating that only warms the rooms you’re in, and screens that switch off when you’ve wandered away. All three double as Bluetooth proxies, too, extending Home Assistant’s Bluetooth range around your home.

The devices certified to the program are:

  • Everything Presence Lite – A more affordable mmWave sensor that tracks up to three people across four zones you set up yourself, bringing multi-zone presence detection to every room.
  • Everything Presence One – Combines mmWave presence, PIR motion, temperature, humidity, and light sensing in one ESPHome device, covering everything a room automation needs from a single sensor.
  • Everything Presence Pro – A professional-grade sensor with two mmWave radars (long-range static and multi-target tracking), PIR motion and light sensing, and built for wired reliability in larger spaces and professional installs.

The most recent addition to the range, the Everything Presence Pro, stands out for pairing 802.3af Power over Ethernet (PoE) with Ethernet. This means that a single cable carries both power and data, so installers can mount it in a ceiling like a Wi-Fi access point or security camera, with no Wi-Fi dropouts or power outlet to worry about.

Want to check out other nifty devices like these? Head to our certified device list to see everything on offer.

Everything, everywhere, all at once

Wi-Fi or wired, all three sensors do everything they need entirely within your home. But if you’d like to check in from afar, Home Assistant Link (formerly Home Assistant Cloud) lets you see which rooms are occupied, or whether the heating’s still on in an empty house, from wherever you are. Best of all, every subscription directly funds the Open Home Foundation – the non-profit behind Home Assistant, ESPHome, and this program – helping us bring more partners like Everything Smart Home on board.

On our radar

Everything Smart Home’s story shows what’s possible with the power of community. Like so many of you, Lewis started out as a home automation enthusiast, and went from recapping our releases to building hardware of his own. With Dave’s engineering know-how and the support of fellow tinkerers, they’ve turned a passion project into a family-led hardware company that we’re thrilled to welcome to the program. We can’t wait to see what they build next 👀

FAQs

Q: If I have a device that is not listed under Works with Home Assistant does this mean it’s not supported?

A: No! It just means that it hasn’t gone through a testing schedule with our team or doesn’t fit the requirements of the program. It might function perfectly well but be added to the testing schedule later down the road, or it might work under a different connectivity type that we don’t currently test under the program.

Q: OK, so what’s the point of the Works with program?

A: It highlights the devices we know work well with Home Assistant and the brands that make a long-term commitment to keeping support for these devices going. The certification agreement specifies that the devices must have the functionality you would expect within Home Assistant, operate locally without the need for cloud, and that they will continue to do so long-term.

Q: How were these devices tested?

A: Everything Smart Home’s certified devices were tested using Home Assistant over a standard Wi-Fi connection. If you have another setup that’s not a problem, but we test this way as it’s the most effective method for our team to certify within our ecosystem.

Q: Will you be adding more Everything Smart Home devices to the program?

A: Why not! We’re thrilled to foster a close relationship with the team at Everything Smart Home to work together on any upcoming releases or add in further products that are not yet listed here.

articles.author: Home Assistant contributors
articles.title: “What the Heck?!” 2026: Everyone at home gets a say
articles.excerpt: All of November is the Month of “What the Heck?!” Tell us what makes Home Assistant hard, confusing, or annoying for you in the WTH category on our forum. Everyone is welcome, and this year we’d love to hear from new and non-technical users, and people living in homes where someone else set it all up. Run Home Assistant yourself? Ask the people you live with how they feel about it!
articles.content:
Home Assistant contributors · Home Assistant · CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

TL;DR

All of November is the Month of “What the Heck?!” Tell us what makes Home Assistant hard, confusing, or annoying for you in the WTH category on our forum. Everyone is welcome, and this year we’d love to hear from new and non-technical users, and people living in homes where someone else set it all up. Run Home Assistant yourself? Ask the people you live with how they feel about it!

Let me start with a confession.

I work on Home Assistant all day, for a living. And still, my own home has moments where the people I live with look at me and go: “What the heck?!”

My most recent one? Profile pictures.

For the longest time, your own profile picture in Home Assistant wasn’t actually yours to change. Only an administrator could do it, tucked away in the settings. So if someone in our house wanted a different picture, they had to ask me, every time. For something that is literally your face, that’s a bit odd, isn’t it?

As of Home Assistant 2026.10, every user, administrator or not, can change their own picture straight from their profile. A tiny change, right? Well, my 13-year-old daughter Lilly now changes hers about every week. I’ve officially lost my job as household profile picture administrator. Best demotion ever 😄

Such a small thing, but it made a big difference in how at home she feels in Home Assistant. And that’s the kind of thing we easily overlook when working on it every day.

So, guess what? It’s that time again. For the whole of November, we’re running the Month of “What the Heck?!” 🎉

Wait, what is this again?

We always value your feedback, but don’t often ask for the tough kind outright. That changes this November. For one month, we open the floodgates. No technical words needed, no fancy format. Just one simple question: what in Home Assistant makes you go “what the heck?!”

The setting you can never find. The moment your home did something and nobody in the household had any clue why. The thing you keep missing, and can’t believe isn’t here yet. All those little (and sometimes not so little) frustrations you’ve quietly learned to live with.

We want to hear them. All of them.

We only do this once every two years, and that’s on purpose. Two years is long enough for a lot to change, in Home Assistant itself and the smart home world around it. The technology moves on, and so do our expectations of what a smart home should do. What bugged you last time might be long gone, and something new might be driving you nuts today.

Why we are doing this

This year, the Open Home Foundation has been focusing on making Home Assistant more approachable. In other words: Home Assistant should not only work for the person who set it up. It should work for everyone who lives in the home.

We’ve made good progress so far. But let’s be real: the people building Home Assistant are pretty bad at spotting what’s confusing about Home Assistant. We know where everything is. We know the workarounds. We stopped being confused years ago.

That makes us terrible test subjects. You, on the other hand, are perfect. And so is everyone in your home.

So this is your month. Complain (nicely), discuss, dream out loud, and tell us what would make Home Assistant better for you.

This year, we want to hear from everyone

Previous editions of WTH month were great. But most of what we heard came from a very specific group: the tinkerers. The people who write YAML for fun, run a dozen apps, and know what an entity ID is.

I’m one of you. We are lovely people. Please keep the WTHs coming 😄

But this year, I want to explicitly invite everybody else too.

  • You just started with Home Assistant. Everything is still fresh, and that “huh?” feeling you had during setup is gold to us. Write it down before you get used to it!
  • You don’t consider yourself a “technical” person. You use Home Assistant, but you don’t want to tinker with it. You want things to just work. Tell us where it doesn’t feel that way.
  • You live in a home where someone else runs Home Assistant. Your partner, parent, room-mate, or child set it all up, and now you live with it, every day. Do you ever feel a little locked out of your own home? This is the group we hear from least, and probably the one we can learn the most from. Home Assistant runs entire households, and most people in those households never open a settings page.

Homework for those of us who run Home Assistant at home

If you’re the one who maintains Home Assistant in your household, I have a small favor to ask.

Go ask the people you live with how they feel about it.

Not “is it working?” because they’ll politely say yes. Ask them for real. Fair warning: you might not like all the answers. I certainly didn’t. But there’s so much to learn from that conversation. Some questions to get it going:

  • What’s the one thing about using Home Assistant that annoys you most?
  • Can you find what you need in the app or on the dashboard? Where do you get lost?
  • When Home Assistant does something unexpected, do you understand why? And what do you do about it? (Is the answer “call you”? Yeah, thought so.)
  • Is there something you’d like to do or change in Home Assistant yourself, but you don’t know how (or don’t dare to)?
  • If you could change one thing about Home Assistant, what would it be?

Then bring what you hear to the forum. Even better: help them post it themselves, in their own words. Their words are exactly what we need.

How it works

All WTHs go into the Month of “What the Heck?!” category on our community forum. To keep things useful (and fun) for everyone, a few simple guidelines:

  • Search first, then vote. Someone may have beaten you to it. Give their topic a vote – it tells us how common a problem is – and add your own story in a reply. Every story adds context.
  • One WTH per topic. That makes it possible to discuss, vote on, and track each one.
  • Describe the moment, not the solution. Tell us what happened, what you expected, and why it bugged you. You don’t need to know how to fix it, and you don’t need any technical words. “I wanted to turn off the kitchen lights and couldn’t figure out where they were in the app” is a perfect WTH.
  • Be kind. We are all here because we care about Home Assistant, our homes, and the people in them. That includes the people working on Home Assistant, many of whom are volunteers, doing this in their spare time.

The category is open for the whole of November.

What happens next?

We read all the WTHs. Yes, really.

In past editions, contributors picked up WTHs and fixed them while the month was still running. I would love to see that happen again. If you’re a contributor and spot one you can tackle: go for it!

Beyond the quick fixes, everything you share helps us understand where Home Assistant needs to go next. It shapes how we make Home Assistant approachable for everyone, not just the person holding the admin account.

So, what the heck?!

Whether you’ve been running Home Assistant since the early days, installed it last week, or simply live with someone who won’t stop talking about it: this month is for you.

Tell us what makes Home Assistant hard, what makes you sigh, or what it’s like to live with it.

Head over to the forum and share your WTH!

I’m looking forward to reading every single one of them (well… at least I’ll do my very best 😅).

../Frenck

FAQ

Do I need an account to post?

Yes, you need a free account on our community forum. Signing up only takes a minute.

I have multiple things! Should I put them all in a single topic?

No, please create a separate topic for each one. There is no limit on how many WTH topics you can create. Smaller topics are much easier to discuss, vote on, and pick up.

I don’t run Home Assistant myself, someone else in my home does. Can I still post?

Yes, please! You are exactly who we’d love to hear from this year. You don’t need to know how it all works behind the scenes; just tell us what it’s like to live with it.

I’m posting on behalf of someone in my home. Is that OK?

Absolutely. Just mention that it comes from them, and use their words as much as you can. How they describe it tells us a lot.

English isn’t my first language. Can I still join?

Of course! The forum is in English, but don’t let that stop you. Feel free to use AI or a translation tool to translate your WTH. If you do, please say so in your post, and add your original text in a hidden details block below it, like this:

[details="Original text"]
Your text in your own language.
[/details]

That way, nothing gets lost in translation, and people can always check what you originally meant. This is the same approach we use in our AI policy.

Does it have to be about Home Assistant itself? What about the mobile Companion app, the documentation, or the website?

All of it counts. If it’s part of your Home Assistant experience, it’s a valid WTH.

My WTH from the last edition still isn’t solved. Can I post it again?

Yes! This is a new edition, and a lot has changed since then. Please create a new WTH, and feel free to link to the old one.

Is everything that is reported going to be fixed?

No, there is no guarantee for that. The goal is to make it easy to tell us what bugs you, for one whole month. What you share helps us understand where Home Assistant is hard, and helps shape what we work on next.

My WTH is one of the top-voted ones, so it’s going to be fixed, right?

This is not a popularity contest. Votes help us see how many people run into the same thing, but they don’t guarantee anything gets picked up.

I really want a new integration or app, so I can use my devices. Is this the right place?

No, this event is not for requesting new integrations or apps. Please open a feature request on GitHub for that.

I found a bug, and I’m comfortable with GitHub. Where should I report it?

If you are comfortable using GitHub, please file an issue there instead. That way, it ends up directly with the people who can fix it, and we can track its progress too.

I’m a contributor and want to fix a WTH. How do I let people know?

Awesome! Reply in the WTH topic and link to your pull request. That way, everyone following the topic knows something is happening.
