articles.title: Naming things in Home Assistant, shaped by your feedback
articles.excerpt: Just before the 2026.4 release, we pulled a change to entity naming in Home Assistant. You’d tested it in beta, told us what you didn’t like, and we listened. It took a few extra months, but we believe it’s now in a better place.
articles.content:
Home Assistant contributors · Home Assistant · CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

Just before the 2026.4 release, we pulled a change to entity naming in Home Assistant. You’d tested it in beta, told us what you didn’t like, and we listened. It took a few extra months, but we believe it’s now in a better place.

We’ve filled the gaps you found, including screens that didn’t show enough context. We’ve also added child devices, which give each part of a device – like sockets on a power strip – its own name and area.

Crucially, your entity IDs, automations, scripts, scenes, and dashboards will keep working.

What is changing from tomorrow’s 2026.11 release is that naming in Home Assistant will be simpler: you’ll name each device and entity for what it actually is, and Home Assistant will add the context around it.

The first place you’ll likely notice this is on your dashboards and other screens. They will build each name from its parts, such as the area, device, and entity name, which means some names will include more context than before.

We know many of you spend hours getting your names just right. Most will carry over the way you expect. Some will look different: particularly any entity names that don’t currently start with their device name. Further down, we explain why, and how to tidy them up quickly.

But before we go on, one thing we heard a lot during beta was that the naming terminology was confusing. Device name, entity name, friendly name, entity ID: what’s the difference? Here’s a quick guide.

What’s in a name?

Let’s say a smart plug powers your coffee machine, and sits in your kitchen.

  • Area: the room/space the smart plug is in. Kitchen.
  • Device: the physical object. Smart plug 3, or a name you give it, like Coffee machine.
  • Entity: a thing a device can do or measure. The smart plug has three entities: a switch, a power sensor and an energy sensor.

Each entity has its own name, ID, and friendly name. So for the smart plug’s power sensor:

  • Entity name: the name of that one thing. Power.
  • Entity ID: the fixed ID your automations use. sensor.kitchen_smart_plug_3_power.
  • Friendly name: a state attribute that combines the device name and entity name. Older cards and templates still use this, but we are moving away from it. Smart plug 3 Power.

Where naming comes from

How did we end up with so many names? It all started simply enough…

In the early days, Home Assistant only knew entities. There were no devices, areas, or floors, so an entity’s name had to carry all its context. To tell power sensors apart, you would name one “Kitchen coffee machine power.” The community wrote whole naming strategy guides to keep them consistent.

From 2018 on, Home Assistant started adding structure around entities. Entities belonging to one physical object were grouped together as a device. Areas, floors, and labels were added to describe the layout of your home. But this structure also introduced repetition, so if you moved the coffee machine to another room, every one of its entity names was wrong.

To fix this, integrations started naming each entity on its own, without the device name. An integration named an entity for what it was, such as “Power,” and Home Assistant put the device name in front to show “Smart plug 3 Power.”

One gap remained: renaming an entity removed its device name. If you renamed a smart plug’s switch to “Coffee machine,” the device’s other entities might still be displayed as “Smart plug 3 Power” and “Smart plug 3 Energy.” As a result, many of you had to rename every entity manually to stay consistent.

At a glance:

Year What arrived What it meant for names
2013 Entities, configured in YAML One name per entity, carrying all the context
2018 Entity registry and devices Entities renamed in the UI; devices group entities
2019 Areas The area is known, but often still typed into names
2022 Entity naming for integrations Integrations name entities standalone; the device name is added in front
2024 Floors and labels More context available, still repeated in names
2026 Child devices and this migration Every name stands on its own, renamed or not

Each of these steps made sense at the time, but together they left us with rules that didn’t always agree. We’ve been untangling them for several years, and this release is the next step.

Where we’re heading

From now on, a consistent set of rules applies everywhere in Home Assistant, from the dashboard to the settings pages. You name each thing once, for what it is: your floor is “Ground floor,” your area “Kitchen,” your device “Coffee machine,” and its entities “Power” and “Energy.” No name repeats another.

Home Assistant will then show context as required:

  • On the Kitchen’s area page, the area is already clear, so the device is listed as just “Coffee machine,” not “Kitchen coffee machine.”
  • On the Coffee machine’s device page, the header already names the device and its area, so the entities are listed as just “Power” and “Energy.”
  • In an entity picker that lists every power sensor in the house, each row also shows the device and area, so you can tell them apart.
  • On a dashboard card, you pick which parts to show: entity, device, parent device, area, or floor, in the order you like.

Some entities need no name of their own. The plug’s switch is what turns the coffee machine on and off, so will be shown with the device name alone: “Coffee machine.” We call it the main entity of the device, and you’ll be able to turn this on for any entity with the “Main entity of the device” switch in its settings. This is why renaming the device, rather than the switch, gives most people the result they want.

A device made of several parts will now get a separate child device for each one. For example, a power strip with four sockets becomes one device with four child devices, one for each socket. Each socket can have its own name, such as “Kettle,” and its own area, instead of entities called “Socket 3,” etc. Put a socket in another area, such as a lamp in the dining room, and it will just show as “Lamp” there, without the power strip’s name.

Our goal is for you to no longer need a naming scheme to keep things tidy. The defaults should be right, and if you do want to rename something you’ll only need to do it once, in one place, because no name holds a copy of another. You can still name things however you like. If an area isn’t specific enough, because you have two spotlights in one kitchen for example, you can keep that detail in the device name: “Cabinet spotlight” and “Countertop spotlight.”

New entity IDs are built from these parts too: since 2026.8, they include the area, and if you really want, you can choose which parts go into them. So two “TV” devices in different rooms get clear IDs, without the _2.

What this means for you

From the 2026.11 release, the change will show up in four main ways.

Dashboards show the new names

Cards, badges, and rows without a manually set name will show the new default entity name together with its context, instead of the friendly name. When you set a name on a card, the name picker lets you pick the parts you want. You can always revert to the default with one click. Names you have already set on a card stay exactly as they are. The rest of Home Assistant follows the same rules: settings pages, the activity log, automation descriptions, voice assistant settings, the tools pages, and the map – as well as the Home Assistant apps for Android and iOS.

Renaming an entity only names the entity

When you rename an entity, you’ll only need to provide a name for the entity part, such as “Power usage,” nothing else. Home Assistant will keep that name just as you typed it, and add the context, such as the device or area name, where it is needed. If what you really want to change is the device name, you will need to rename the device instead.

Complex devices are split into child devices

From this release, Z-Wave, MQTT, and ESPHome will support the child devices described above, as will some Tuya devices and a few other integrations. Support for Matter and ZHA is in progress, with more integrations to follow. As a result the original parent device will remain, but its structural elements – like multiple outlets on a power strip – will be split into child devices that are organized separately from one another.

The friendly name is on its way out

Many custom cards and templates still use the friendly name. We’ll keep it for backward compatibility for now, but plan to deprecate the friendly name and eventually remove it. We’ll announce any removal ahead of time, so card authors and template users can update first.

Things to check after updating

What to expect after the update, and some things you may want to look out for.

Entity IDs, automations, and dashboards will keep working

Existing entity IDs will not change. Automations, scripts, scenes, and dashboards refer to entities by their ID, so they’ll keep finding the right entity. Only the names you see may change, as described below.

Your existing names will be migrated

On update, Home Assistant will migrate the names of entities you renamed in the past. As we mentioned at the start, most should come through as you’d expect, but some may look different. It depends on how the name starts:

  1. If an entity name already starts with its device name, such as “Coffee machine power usage” on a coffee machine, the device part will be removed – so the entity will now be named “Power usage,” and show as “Coffee machine Power usage,” much as before.
  2. If it does not already start with its device name, nothing changes except Home Assistant will add the right context where needed – so a switch you renamed “Coffee machine” on the device “Smart plug 3” will show as “Smart plug 3 Coffee machine.”

If that second case looks odd, it’s quick to fix. Rename the device (in this case the smart plug) to “Coffee machine” and turn on “Main entity of the device” for the switch. Then it will show as just “Coffee machine” everywhere. If you have time, it might also be a good moment to take area names out of your entity and device names. Home Assistant will display the right content where needed.

For entities you expose to Assist, Alexa, or Google Assistant, the old name will also be added as an alias, so voice commands keep working.

Our naming documentation explains how naming works, and what you may want to rename, in more detail.

Some custom cards may show different names

Built-in cards will let you compose the name from parts: drag entity, device, parent device, area, and floor into the order you want, or type your own custom name. Some custom cards may still read the friendly name, so might show a different name than the built-in cards, and that name will change once you rename the entity or its device. Set the name on the card to fix it, or update the card once its author supports the new naming.

Templates using friendly names may need changing

If your templates still use friendly names, for example to show entity names in notifications, those names may differ from what Home Assistant shows, and change once you rename the entity or its device. To pick only the parts you need, use entity_name(), device_name() and area_name() instead.

What’s next?

We know naming is personal, and this change touches every installation – even if for many users it won’t be noticeable. It won’t be perfect for every setup, but we’re confident it’s a change for the better. Over the coming releases, we’ll keep moving more integrations to child devices and helping custom card authors adopt the new naming.

To everyone who tested the 2026.4 beta, reported issues, and told us honestly what you thought: thank you. You made this change better.

One more ask: if something looks off after updating, tell us. As always, you’ll find us on the community forums or on Discord.

articles.title: 2026.11: A lot in store!
articles.excerpt: This is the biggest release we’ve ever shipped, by far. It’s ridiculously large. 🤯 A huge shout-out to everyone who helped make it happen, thank you! ❤️
articles.content:
Home Assistant contributors · Home Assistant · CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

Home Assistant 2026.11! 🎉

This is the biggest release we’ve ever shipped, by far. It’s ridiculously large. 🤯 A huge shout-out to everyone who helped make it happen, thank you! ❤️

For years, HACS, the Home Assistant Community Store, has been the place to find custom integrations, dashboard cards, and themes made by the community. Starting with this release, it’s built right into Home Assistant as the new Marketplace. I’ve been working on bringing it over myself, and my goal was simple: if you use HACS today, it should feel like only the name changed. Everything you installed stays installed and keeps getting updates. And if you never tried HACS because installing it felt like a hurdle, that hurdle is gone: it’s simply there, under Settings, on every installation type. 🛍️

None of this would exist without @ludeeus, who started HACS and donated it to the Open Home Foundation, and all the maintainers and developers who built that ecosystem over the years. 🙏 And this is just the first version of what a marketplace for Home Assistant could become.

You know by now I’m an automation person, so I’m also very happy you can finally exclude items from a target. Turn on all the lights downstairs, except the one in the kitchen? Done. And it stays smart: add another light to the kitchen next month, and it’s left out too. 🧠

Then there’s naming. More than four years in the making, entity naming got a complete rethink: you name a thing once, and Home Assistant adds the context where it helps. Welcome to the Marketplace

For years, the community has built custom integrationsA custom integration is an integration that has been created by someone from the Home Assistant community and has been published for others to use at their own risk. Custom integrations are not supported by the Home Assistant project. They are not reviewed or tested by the Home Assistant development team and thus may negatively impact the stability of your Home Assistant instance. An example of a custom integration is the Spook integration., dashboard cards, themes, and templates for Home Assistant. People found them through HACS, the Home Assistant Community Store. With this release, HACS becomes part of Home Assistant as the new Marketplace.

The Marketplace brings the existing HACS experience into Home Assistant and the regular release process. It works with every installation type, including Home Assistant ContainerHome Assistant Container is a standalone container-based installation of Home Assistant Core. Any OCI compatible runtime can be used, but the documentation focus is on Docker. [Learn more], without manually downloading or unpacking files. Everything in the Marketplace is free, and that will not change.

Browse and install

You can find the Marketplace under Settings > Marketplace. It comes with Home Assistant, so there is nothing to set up. As an administrator, you can browse the catalog and install integrations, dashboard cards, themes, and templates. You do not need a GitHub account to install or update projects.

Installing a new integrationIntegrations connect and integrate Home Assistant with your devices, services, and more. [Learn more] got shorter, too. In HACS, you downloaded it, restarted Home Assistant, went to Devices & services, and searched for it again to set it up. In the Marketplace, you select Install, and you land straight in its setup flow, without a restart. Updates still need a restart for now.

The page of each project now shows more than its README: how often it was downloaded, its stars on GitHub, and the Home Assistant version it requires, so you know what you’re getting into before you install.

Every project you install gets an “update entity”An update entity is an entity that indicates if an update is available for a device or service. [Learn more], so updates show up under Settings > Updates, next to the updates of Home Assistant itself. After an update, a repair tells you when a restart is needed, and can restart Home Assistant for you.

The first time you open the Marketplace, it shows a notice. Everything in the Marketplace is made by the community. It is not tested, audited, or supported by the Home Assistant project, and it runs inside your Home Assistant. Read the notice, select I understand the risks and agree, and you’re in. Browsing works before that. Installing and updating does not.

The Marketplace adds several improvements:

  • Group the Browse and Installed lists by status, type, or source. Home Assistant remembers your grouping.
  • Filter by source to distinguish the community catalog from custom repositories.
  • Select multiple repositories on the Installed tab and uninstall them at once.
  • Skipped updates no longer keep a repository at the top of the list or count in the update badge. A new release makes the update available again.
  • Search, filters, and sorting are saved in the URL, so you can share a link to a specific Marketplace view.
  • Integrations show their brand images before you install them.

Custom repositories

Not every project is in the catalog. To add one that is missing, select Add from link and enter its repository URL. The Marketplace then lists it with your other repositories.

The Custom repositories page lists repositories you added this way and lets you open or remove them. A repository stays in the list until you uninstall it.

Custom repositories require a GitHub connection. The Marketplace uses GitHub device sign-in, so you approve the connection on GitHub without entering your password in Home Assistant. The connection only reads public information and cannot access private repositories.

Where your downloads come from

By default, the Marketplace gets its catalog and everything you install from GitHub. Where GitHub cannot be reached, such as in mainland China, you can switch to the mirrors run by the Home Assistant China community. Go to Settings > Marketplace, select the three dots menu in the upper-right corner, and select Download source. If the Marketplace cannot reach the catalog and a mirror is available for your country, a repair suggests it.

Everything the Marketplace downloads then goes through whoever runs that mirror, and through a third-party proxy whenever those mirrors cannot be reached: the catalog, and the code you install. Only pick a download source you trust. If you used the Chinese version of HACS, the Marketplace selects these mirrors for you when it migrates.

HACS made this possible. @ludeeus founded it and donated it to the Open Home Foundation about a year and a half ago, which is what made bringing it into Home Assistant possible. Together with the HACS maintainers and the many developers publishing their projects, he built the ecosystem that the Marketplace now carries forward. Thank you. ❤️

If you use HACS today, there is nothing you need to do. Home Assistant migrates it when it starts after the update. Everything you installed stays installed and keeps receiving updates, your custom repositories and update entities carry over, and links and bookmarks that point to HACS now open the Marketplace.

The HACS installer stops at Home Assistant 2026.11, so a separate HACS installation is no longer possible on this version. The old HACS won’t get new releases either: the Marketplace ships with every Home Assistant update. Everything you need to know about the move, for users and for publishers, is in the Marketplace documentation.

This is a starting point, and the first version of what a marketplace for Home Assistant could become. Got ideas? Share them in the Marketplace section of the feature request discussions on GitHub. Found a bug? Report it in the Home Assistant issue tracker, not in the HACS repository.

Name it once, Home Assistant adds the context

Name a thing once, and Home Assistant makes sure it makes sense everywhere. That is the idea behind how entitiesAn entity represents a sensor, actor, or function in Home Assistant. Entities are used to monitor physical properties or to control other entities. An entity is usually part of a device or a service. [Learn more] are named from this release on, and it has been more than four years in the making. You give an entity its own name, like “Temperature”. Home Assistant knows which deviceA device is a model representing a physical or logical unit that contains entities. it belongs to, and in which areaAn area in Home Assistant is a logical grouping of devices and entities that represents a room or space in your home, such as the living room, kitchen, or garage. [Learn more] that device lives, so it can add that context where it helps. By default, that is the name of the device: the “Temperature” of a “Thermostat” in the “Bedroom” shows up as “Thermostat Temperature”. Where you want more, a card can add the area too, like “Bedroom Thermostat Temperature”.

Naming has been a topic in the community for years, with threads like “How do you name your devices?” and “Naming strategies for entities?”, all looking for a system that keeps a growing home readable.

It’s time to let those systems go. You shouldn’t need a strategy to make sense of the information in Home Assistant. Home Assistant should give you the context you need, at the moment you need it. Now you rename the device, and every entity on it follows. Entities you renamed, and entities you never touched, get their context the same way.

You see this in dashboards, settings, the activity and logbook, the voice assistant settings, and the apps. The same name, in the same structure, everywhere you look.

A few things to know:

  • Renaming an entity only renames the entity. If you want to change the name of the device, rename the device. If an entity represents the main function of its device, turn on Main entity of the device in its settings, and it goes by the name and the area of the device.
  • Devices with multiple parts, like a power strip, now get a deviceA device is a model representing a physical or logical unit that contains entities. per part, each with its own name and areaAn area in Home Assistant is a logical grouping of devices and entities that represents a room or space in your home, such as the living room, kitchen, or garage. [Learn more]. These are called child devices. A child device inherits the area of its parent, until you give it one of its own. Integrations are moving to them one by one, starting with the multi-channel switches in Tuya.
  • Your own names are kept. Home Assistant migrates names you set. If an entity’s displayed name changes, the old name remains an alias for voice assistants. For example, “turn on the ceiling light” continues to work.
  • Templates: The friendly_name attribute is planned for deprecation. Use entity_name(), device_name(), and area_name() to build the name you need.

What doesn’t change: entity IDs. Your automationsAutomations in Home Assistant allow you to automatically respond to things that happen in and around your home. [Learn more], scriptsA script is a saved list of steps that runs when you start it, for example, from a dashboard, with Assist, or from an automation. Unlike an automation, a script has no triggers, so it doesn’t start by itself. [Learn more], and dashboards keep working.

We are upfront about one thing: this is a backward-incompatible change. Some names look different after the update, and you notice that most on your dashboards. Cards, badges, and rows without a name now show the device name followed by the entity name, instead of the friendly name. Making them shorter is quick: rename the device or the entity, turn on Main entity of the device for the entity that represents the device, or set a name on the card. The details are in the backward-incompatible changes below.

Store backups and media on local drives

“Backups”Home Assistant has built-in functionality to create files containing a copy of your configuration. This can be used to restore your Home Assistant as well as migrate to a new system. The backup feature is available for all installation types. [Learn more] and media take up a lot of space, and the best place for them is often not the drive Home Assistant runs on. Besides network storage, you can now add an internal drive or a USB drive. Go to Settings > System > Storage, select Add storage, and select Local disk as the type. Use it for backups, media, or shared files, just like network storage. Home Assistant remembers the disk by its file system identifier, so it keeps working after a restart or when the device name changes, and a repair tells you if the disk is disconnected. The disk needs to be formatted already. For the supported file systems and all the details, refer to the local disk storage documentation.

Backups got a few more improvements. Restoring no longer makes a temporary copy of the whole backup first, which saves free space and time, especially for backups on network storage. The progress bar on the backup page now fills as the backup uploads, and Dropbox, Azure Storage, SFTP Storage, Synology DSM, and Backblaze B2 now report their upload progress too. And the new Last successful automatic backup size sensorSensors return information about a thing, for instance the level of water in a tank. [Learn more] lets you keep an eye on how big your automatic backups are, so you can get notified when they suddenly grow or shrink.

Thanks, @MindFreeze, @agners, @KapJI, and @erwindouna!

Reach the far corners with LoRaWAN

LoRaWAN is a long-range, low-power wireless protocol, often used for battery-powered sensors in places your Wi-Fi never reaches, like a garden, a shed, or a field. Home Assistant now speaks it. Connect your LoRaWAN network server, ChirpStack or The Things Network, and Home Assistant offers the matching device integrationIntegrations connect and integrate Home Assistant with your devices, services, and more. [Learn more], like SenseCAP, when a supported device shows up.

All of it comes together in a new LoRaWAN page in Settings > Connectivity. It shows your connections and how many devicesA device is a model representing a physical or logical unit that contains entities. each has, and a table of all your devices that you can search and filter by connection. A map shows how your network hangs together: which gateways receive which devices, and which devices no gateway has seen. On the page of a device, you find its radio details, like signal strength, the last time it reported in, and its battery. A device that Home Assistant doesn’t support yet still shows up, with a note on what is missing. And when you want to add a new device, Home Assistant takes you straight to the management console of its connection.

Thanks, @balloob!

Batteryless switches with Zigbee Green Power

Zigbee Home Automation now supports Zigbee Green Power. Green Power devicesA device is a model representing a physical or logical unit that contains entities. run without a battery: a wall switch powered by the energy of your press, or a sensor that lives off the light in the room. Friends of Hue switches are the best-known example. Until now, Home Assistant passed them by.

They work differently from other Zigbee devices, and the interface follows along. A Green Power device lists its Source ID with its network details, and the options that don’t apply to it, like reconfiguring it or managing its clusters, are left out. In the network visualization it shows up without a line to a parent, because a Green Power device doesn’t have one.

Thanks, @puddly!

Matter covers that can only tilt, without moving up and down, such as tilt-only blind controllers, are now shown as tilt covers. Before, their state was always unknown.

They now use the cover.open_cover_tilt, cover.close_cover_tilt, cover.stop_cover_tilt, and cover.toggle_cover_tilt actions, instead of cover.open_cover, cover.close_cover, cover.stop_cover, and cover.toggle. Update automations, scripts, and device actions that use the old actions on these covers. Voice assistants that open or close these covers may also no longer work for them. Covers that can move up and down are not affected.

(@TheJulianJES - #188787) (Matter documentation)

MQTT

MQTT entities without a unique_id no longer use their device configuration. These entities could not be linked to a device, but a via_device in their device configuration still created a device in the device registry. That device is no longer created. To link an MQTT entity to a device, add a unique_id to the entity.

(@jbouwh - #187856) (MQTT documentation)

Nanoleaf

The deprecated Nanoleaf touch gesture device triggers have been removed. Automations using a Nanoleaf device trigger (single tap, double tap, swipe up/down/left/right) will no longer work. Use the Touch gesture event entityAn event entity represents a momentary occurrence without a lasting state, for example, when you press a doorbell or a button on a remote control. Instead of a state such as on or off, the event entity keeps track of when the last event was detected and its event type, such as a single press or a long press. [Learn more] of your Nanoleaf device instead, for example with an event.received trigger on the event entity filtered by its event_type attribute.

The device triggers were deprecated in Home Assistant 2024.7 and scheduled for removal in 2025.1.

(@MartinHjelmare - #188656) (Nanoleaf documentation)

NINA

The NINA attributes that were deprecated in Home Assistant 2026.5 have been removed. Each one has an entityAn entity represents a sensor, actor, or function in Home Assistant. Entities are used to monitor physical properties or to control other entities. An entity is usually part of a device or a service. [Learn more] or an actionAn action makes Home Assistant do something, for example, turn on a light, send a notification, or activate a scene. Automations and scripts run a list of actions. [Learn more] that takes its place:

  • headline: the Headline sensor
  • description: the nina.get_details action
  • sender: the Sender sensor
  • severity: the Severity sensor
  • recommended_actions: the nina.get_details action
  • affected_areas: the Affected areas sensor for the shortened list, or the nina.get_details action for the full one
  • web: the More information URL sensor
  • sent: the Sent sensor
  • start: the Start sensor
  • expires: the Expires sensor

Update automationsAutomations in Home Assistant allow you to automatically respond to things that happen in and around your home. [Learn more], scriptsA script is a saved list of steps that runs when you start it, for example, from a dashboard, with Assist, or from an automation. Unlike an automation, a script has no triggers, so it doesn’t start by itself. [Learn more], templatesA template is an automation definition that can include variables for the action or data from the trigger values. This allows automations to generate dynamic actions. [Learn more], and dashboard cards that read one of these attributes.

(@DeerMaximum - #188355) (NINA documentation)

Philips Hue

The "None" light effect has been removed. It was deprecated in Home Assistant 2025.4 in favor of "off", and the mapping that kept the old value working is now gone. Update automationsAutomations in Home Assistant allow you to automatically respond to things that happen in and around your home. [Learn more] and scriptsA script is a saved list of steps that runs when you start it, for example, from a dashboard, with Assist, or from an automation. Unlike an automation, a script has no triggers, so it doesn’t start by itself. [Learn more] that set the effect to "None" so that they use "off" instead.

(@MartinHjelmare - #188867) (Philips Hue documentation)

Plaato

The Plaato integration no longer lets you set a custom pollingData polling is the process of querying a device or service at regular intervals to check for updates or retrieve data. By defining a custom polling interval, you can control how frequently your system checks for new data, which can help optimize performance and reduce unnecessary network traffic. [Learn more] interval. If you configured one, it is ignored and the default interval is used.

(@tr4nt0r - #184376) (Plaato documentation)

Python dependencies

Home Assistant no longer installs Python packages into the deps folder of your configuration directory. This only affects Home Assistant CoreHome Assistant Core is the Python program at the heart of Home Assistant. It is part of all installation types. It can be installed standalone (without Home Assistant Supervisor) as a container using Docker (this is typically referred to as the Home Assistant Container installation type). For development, Core can also be run using a Virtual Environment (previously referred as the Home Assistant Core installation type). For production setup, the Home Assistant Core installation type is deprecated. installations that run outside a virtual environment, which is where that folder was used. Run Home Assistant Core in a virtual environment, as the installation instructions describe, and the packages are installed there instead.

Home Assistant Operating SystemHome Assistant OS, the Home Assistant Operating System, is an embedded, minimalistic, operating system designed to run the Home Assistant ecosystem on single board computers (like the Raspberry Pi) or Virtual Machines. It includes Home Assistant Core, the Home Assistant Supervisor, and supports apps. Home Assistant Supervisor keeps it up to date, removing the need for you to manage an operating system. Home Assistant Operating System is the recommended installation type for most users., Home Assistant SupervisedThe Home Assistant Supervised installation type is a full UI managed home automation ecosystem that runs the Home Assistant Core program, the Home Assistant Supervisor and apps. It comes pre-installed on Home Assistant OS, but can be installed standalone on Debian Linux systems. It leverages Docker, which is managed by the Home Assistant Supervisor. The Home Assistant Supervised installation type is deprecated., and Home Assistant ContainerHome Assistant Container is a standalone container-based installation of Home Assistant Core. Any OCI compatible runtime can be used, but the documentation focus is on Docker. [Learn more] are not affected. Once you have updated, you can remove the deps folder from your configuration directory.

(@emontnemery - #168155)

Ring

Several Ring entities that were deprecated in Home Assistant 2024.9, and originally scheduled for removal in Home Assistant 2025.4, have now been removed:

  • The ding and motion binary sensors, and the last ding and last motion sensors. Use the event entities instead.
  • The volume sensors, including the doorbell, microphone, and voice volume sensors. Use the number entities instead, which also let you change the volume.
  • The siren switch. Use the siren entity instead.

If you use any of these entities in an automation, script, or dashboard, update it to use its replacement.

(@tr4nt0r - #187592) (@tr4nt0r - #187596) (@tr4nt0r - #188108) (Ring documentation)

Risco

The Risco integration no longer lets you set a custom pollingData polling is the process of querying a device or service at regular intervals to check for updates or retrieve data. By defining a custom polling interval, you can control how frequently your system checks for new data, which can help optimize performance and reduce unnecessary network traffic. [Learn more] interval. If you configured one, it is ignored and the default interval is used.

(@tr4nt0r - #184386) (Risco documentation)

Rituals Perfume Genie

The Fill sensor of Rituals Perfume Genie diffusers now reports a percentage, instead of a range as text like “70-80%”. If you use it in automations or scripts, compare it against a number instead. When there is no measurement, it is unknown instead of “No measurement available”.

The Perfume sensor is now unknown when no cartridge is inserted, instead of showing “Cartridge is not loaded”. Use the new Cartridge binary sensor to tell whether a cartridge is inserted.

(@frenck - #186995) (Rituals Perfume Genie documentation)

SMTP

When an attachment cannot be read, the SMTP notify action now reports an error instead of sending the message without it. Before, a missing file was only logged as a warning and the rest of the email went out, so a wrong path could go unnoticed for a long time.

If one of your automationsAutomations in Home Assistant allow you to automatically respond to things that happen in and around your home. [Learn more] or scriptsA script is a saved list of steps that runs when you start it, for example, from a dashboard, with Assist, or from an automation. Unlike an automation, a script has no triggers, so it doesn’t start by itself. [Learn more] attaches a file that is not always there, such as a camera snapshot, check the path, or build the list of attachments so that it only contains files that exist.

(@tr4nt0r - #188876) (SMTP documentation)

Telegram

The legacy Telegram notify platform (notify with platform: telegram in YAML), deprecated in 2025.11, has been removed. Its notify.<name> actions no longer exist.

Use the notify entities of the Telegram bot integration instead: add each chat ID as a subentry of your Telegram bot and send messages with the notify.send_message action, or use the telegram_bot actions for photos, documents, keyboards, and other options. Remove the platform: telegram entries from the notify section of your configuration.yamlThe configuration.yaml file is the main configuration file for Home Assistant. It lists the integrations to be loaded and their specific configurations. In some cases, the configuration needs to be edited manually directly in the configuration.yaml file. Most integrations can be configured in the UI. [Learn more] file. If the configuration is still present, Home Assistant shows a repair issue.

(@jbouwh - #188196) (Telegram documentation)

Telldus Live

The tellduslive YAMLYAML is a human-readable data serialization language. It is used to store and transmit data in a structured format. In Home Assistant, YAML is used for configuration, for example in the configuration.yaml or automations.yaml files. [Learn more] configuration is no longer imported. If you still have a tellduslive: entry in your configuration.yamlThe configuration.yaml file is the main configuration file for Home Assistant. It lists the integrations to be loaded and their specific configurations. In some cases, the configuration needs to be edited manually directly in the configuration.yaml file. Most integrations can be configured in the UI. [Learn more], remove it. Home Assistant raises a repair issue to remind you.

This should not affect anyone in practice: YAML has been imported into a config entry since December 2018, when the config flow was added. Any existing YAML setup was converted long ago and keeps working, and a YAML entry has had no effect since the config entry was created.

(@gjohansson-ST - #185838) (Telldus Live documentation)

Tomorrow.io

The Tomorrow.io integration now has one entry per API key instead of one per location. Each location is a subentry of the entry for its API key. Existing setups migrate automatically and no action is required: locations, entities, devices, and their history are preserved, and per-location “timestep” options carry over. Two things change if you had multiple locations: locations sharing an API key now live under a single config entry, and each location gets its own device. The nowcast timestep is now changed by selecting Reconfigure on a location instead of the integration options.

(@raman325 - #177911) (Tomorrow.io documentation)

Tuya

Multi-channel Tuya devices now put the entitiesAn entity represents a sensor, actor, or function in Home Assistant. Entities are used to monitor physical properties or to control other entities. An entity is usually part of a device or a service. [Learn more] of each channel on their own Channel deviceA device is a model representing a physical or logical unit that contains entities., as a child device of the main one.

Entity IDs and history are kept, and a triggerA trigger is the part of an automation that makes the automation start when something specific happens, for example, when the sun sets, a door opens, or a button is pressed. [Learn more], conditionConditions check whether something is true at that moment, for example, whether a door is closed. You can use them in automations and scripts. If a condition is not met, the actions that come after it in the same sequence do not run. At the top level of an automation or script, this stops the automation or script. [Learn more], or actionAn action makes Home Assistant do something, for example, turn on a light, send a notification, or activate a scene. Automations and scripts run a list of actions. [Learn more] that targets the main device still covers the channel entities. What changes is the name. An entity called “Socket 1” becomes “Socket” on the “Channel 1” device, and its friendly_name attribute is now built from that channel device, so it reads “Channel 1 Socket” instead of the name of the main device followed by “Socket 1”. Single-channel devices go from “Socket 1” to “Socket” as well.

Update templatesA template is an automation definition that can include variables for the action or data from the trigger values. This allows automations to generate dynamic actions. [Learn more], dashboard cards, and notifications that use friendly_name or the old entity name.

(@epenet - #184915) (@epenet - #188169) (@epenet - #188237) (@epenet - #188255) (@epenet - #188258) (@epenet - #188674) (@epenet - #188675) (Tuya documentation)

UniFi Protect

The deprecated UniFi Protect HDR mode switch is removed. It was deprecated in 2024.4 because it cannot represent the auto HDR mode. Use the HDR mode select instead. If an enabled switch is still used in an automation or script, a repair lists the automations and scripts that use it.

(@RaHehl - #184425) (UniFi Protect documentation)

The read-only UniFi Protect UP Sense setting entities deprecated in 2026.9 are removed. Use the matching switch or the “Motion sensitivity” number instead. A repair lists automations and scripts that still use a removed entity.

(@RaHehl - #184473) (UniFi Protect documentation)

Uptime Kuma

Support for Uptime Kuma versions earlier than 2.0.0 has been dropped. Version 2.0.0 was released more than a year ago. Update Uptime Kuma before updating Home Assistant if you use an older version.

(@tr4nt0r - #187418) (Uptime Kuma documentation)

Watergate

The Water meter volume (sensor.<name>_water_meter_volume) and Water meter duration (sensor.<name>_water_meter_duration) sensors of Watergate Sonic now report the positive meter (water flowing in the normal direction) instead of the positive minus negative difference. Entity IDs, unique IDs, and long-term statistics are unchanged.

  • Who is affected: only devices that have ever recorded reverse flow (backflow). The value steps up once, by the device’s lifetime backflow, at the first update after upgrading. Because these sensors are total_increasing, Home Assistant records that step as consumption, so the Energy dashboard and statistics show a one-time spike. Devices with no recorded backflow see no change.
  • How to recover: adjust the spike away with Adjust a statistic in Settings > Tools > Statistics, or ignore it. Nothing needs to be reconfigured.
  • Why: the old value silently hid reverse flow and was not the monotonically increasing total the state class promises. The new Water meter negative volume/duration sensors expose the reverse reading separately.

On firmware that only reports a single (differential) meter, Water meter volume/duration keep reporting that differential and the new negative sensors are unavailable.

(@adam-the-hero - #186035) (Watergate documentation)

Xiaomi BLE

The high and low frequency values of the S400 impedance sensors were swapped. This release corrects the mapping. Entities are not migrated: the scale overwrites its impedance values on every weigh-in, for whichever profile steps on it, so past readings are not tied to a specific user and keeping their history has little value.

After updating:

  • The entity previously exposed as impedance is no longer updated and can be removed.
  • impedance_low now reports the actual low frequency value. It previously reported the high frequency one.
  • impedance_high is a new sensor.

Check automationsAutomations in Home Assistant allow you to automatically respond to things that happen in and around your home. [Learn more], templatesA template is an automation definition that can include variables for the action or data from the trigger values. This allows automations to generate dynamic actions. [Learn more], and dashboards that rely on these entities.

(@dckiller51 - #173260) (Xiaomi BLE documentation)

Xiaomi Home

Xiaomi Miio light, switch, and fan actions now require an explicit target. Previously, calling them without an entity_id acted on every matching Xiaomi Miio device. Calls without a target now fail with a validation error.

Existing calls that specify entity_id still work. To act on all matching entities, use entity_id: all.

This affects these actions in the xiaomi_miio domainEach integration in Home Assistant has a unique identifier: The domain. It is often shown as the first part (before the dot) of entity IDs.:

  • Light: light_set_scene, light_set_delayed_turn_off, light_reminder_on, light_reminder_off, light_night_light_mode_on, light_night_light_mode_off, light_eyecare_mode_on, light_eyecare_mode_off
  • Switch: switch_set_wifi_led_on, switch_set_wifi_led_off, switch_set_power_mode, switch_set_power_price
  • Fan: fan_reset_filter, fan_set_extra_features

(@balloob - #179544) (Xiaomi Home documentation)

Z-Wave

With this release, you will need to update your zwave-js-server instance. You must use zwave-js-server 3.11.0 or greater (schema 51).

  • If you use the Z-Wave JS appApps are additional standalone third-party software packages that can be installed on Home Assistant OS. [Learn more], you need at least version 1.9.0.
  • If you use the Z-Wave JS UI Docker container, you need at least version zwave-js/zwave-js-ui@v11.24.2 (release).
  • If you run your own Docker container or some other installation method, you will need to update your zwave-js-server instance to at least 3.11.0.

(@MartinHjelmare - #184901) (Z-Wave documentation)

Entities for features on non-root endpoints of multi-endpoint Z-Wave devices now live on their own child devicesA device is a model representing a physical or logical unit that contains entities. of the main device, when the Z-Wave JS device database describes those endpoints as separate parts. Only devices with that information are affected: endpoints that carry a label, or that belong to an endpoint group.

Because the name of an entityAn entity represents a sensor, actor, or function in Home Assistant. Entities are used to monitor physical properties or to control other entities. An entity is usually part of a device or a service. [Learn more] is built from the device it belongs to, the name of the main device no longer appears in it. A thermostat with three temperature sensors used to be one device with “Air temperature (2)”, “Air temperature (3)”, and “Air temperature (4)”. It is now a main device with one child device per sensor, each named after its endpoint label, such as “Room Sensor”, and each with a single “Air temperature” entity. A multi-clamp energy meter becomes the main device plus one child device per clamp.

Entity IDs stay the same, and automationsAutomations in Home Assistant allow you to automatically respond to things that happen in and around your home. [Learn more] and scriptsA script is a saved list of steps that runs when you start it, for example, from a dashboard, with Assist, or from an automation. Unlike an automation, a script has no triggers, so it doesn’t start by itself. [Learn more] that target the main device keep working, because targeting a device also targets the entities of its child devices.

One entity does disappear: the redundant endpoint-2 “slat” value of the Fibaro FGR223 and the Shelly Qubino Wave Shutter (QNSH-001P10) is no longer created. If you had enabled that cover entity, it is gone.

(@MartinHjelmare - #185985) (Z-Wave documentation)

Zigbee Home Automation

Each ZHA groupGroups are a way to organize your entities into a single unit. [Learn more] that has group entitiesAn entity represents a sensor, actor, or function in Home Assistant. Entities are used to monitor physical properties or to control other entities. An entity is usually part of a device or a service. [Learn more] now gets its own deviceA device is a model representing a physical or logical unit that contains entities., named after the group, and those entities move there from the coordinator device. Entity IDs and settings are kept, and a name or areaAn area in Home Assistant is a logical grouping of devices and entities that represents a room or space in your home, such as the living room, kitchen, or garage. [Learn more] you set yourself moves along, so automationsAutomations in Home Assistant allow you to automatically respond to things that happen in and around your home. [Learn more], scriptsA script is a saved list of steps that runs when you start it, for example, from a dashboard, with Assist, or from an automation. Unlike an automation, a script has no triggers, so it doesn’t start by itself. [Learn more], and dashboards that use the group entities keep working.

Two things need your attention:

  • If you target the coordinator device to control your groups, target the group entities or the new group devices instead. The device page of the coordinator no longer lists the group entities.
  • If you relied on the group entities being in the area of the coordinator device, give the new group devices or their entities an area of their own.

(@TheJulianJES - #188830) (Zigbee Home Automation documentation)

If you are a custom integrationA custom integration is an integration that has been created by someone from the Home Assistant community and has been published for others to use at their own risk. Custom integrations are not supported by the Home Assistant project. They are not reviewed or tested by the Home Assistant development team and thus may negatively impact the stability of your Home Assistant instance. An example of a custom integration is the Spook integration. developer and want to learn about changes and new features available for your integration: Be sure to follow the blog on our contributors site. The following changes are the most notable for this release:

  • A new home for every contributor
  • A Python console inside Home Assistant
  • Always pass a step_id to flow results
  • Auth providers now opt in to multi-factor authentication
  • Backup agents can now be renamed
  • Climate entities now expose their temperature unit
  • Config entry functions now return None
  • Custom section strategies in the dashboard editor
  • DeviceInfo is now a dataclass
  • Frontend component updates in 2026.11
  • Integrations have categories now
  • Introducing child devices
  • New entity lifecycle hooks
  • New unit of measurement selector
  • Repair issues can belong to a config entry, and be refreshed
  • ScannerEntity now handles devices like other entities
  • Show form fields based on other fields
  • Two-way audio for camera entities
  • Undefined sentinel changes
  • Update entities can customize update availability
  • Water heater entities now expose their temperature unit

All changes

Of course, there is a lot more in this release. You can find a list of all changes made here: Full changelog for Home Assistant Core 2026.11.

articles.excerpt: Something big just happened. As the Open Home Foundation’s Android developer for Home Assistant, I was invited by the European Commission to consult on Android interoperability. articles.title: Making our web analytics open source with Plausible
articles.excerpt: The Open Home Foundation fights for privacy, choice, and sustainability. These principles are at the heart of everything we do, including how we handle website analytics. Our position is clear: we reject tools that track individuals across the web to monetize their data. Instead, we want aggregated, anonymized analytics that show how our websites are performing overall — without identifying who our visitors are, or compromising their privacy.
